papers.title: Contextual Stress Exposure and Longitudinal Change in Mental Health and Sleep Among US Latino/a Adolescents.
papers.abstract: This research examines how contextual stress exposure within the immigration environment predicts sleep problems and internalizing symptoms for Latino/a adolescents. Participants included N = 547 adolescents listed as "Hispanic" on 2017-18 middle school enrollment lists in a suburban Atlanta, GA, school district. Using three time (T) points of survey data (2021-23), structural equation models tested paths from immigration-related stressors to changes in sleep problems and internalizing symptoms. Missing data were addressed using multiply imputed datasets and full information maximum likelihood. At T1, the 244 (44.6%) male and 303 (55.4%) female participants had a mean (SD) age of 16.2 (.91) years. Across time, 28.8%-40.3% of youth reported <7 hours of sleep on average. The prevalence of clinical internalizing symptoms ranged from 31.1% to 35.9% for female participants and from 29.9% to 44.3% for male participants. T1 immigration-related stressors predicted T1 to T2 increases in sleep problems (ß = .12 [95% CI = .03-.20]) and internalizing symptoms (ß = .09 [95% CI = .01-.17]). T2 sleep problems mediated associations between T1 immigration-related stressors and T2 to T3 increases in internalizing symptoms (indirect effect: ß = .01 [95% CI = .00-.03]) and sleep problems (indirect effect: ß = .07 [95% CI = .02-.12]). Sleep problems and internalizing symptoms were reciprocally associated from T1 to T2 (sleep to internalizing: ß = .11 [95% CI = .02-.20]; internalizing to sleep: ß = .14 [95% CI = .04-.25]) and from T2 to T3 (sleep to internalizing: ß = .11 [95% CI = .03-.20]; internalizing to sleep: ß = .10 [95% CI = .00-.20]). For Latino/a adolescents, immigration-related stressors may harm mental health through increased sleep problems.

papers.title: Predictors of Aggression in Children and Adolescents With Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Aggression is a common and impairing co-occurring behavior among children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), negatively affecting developmental outcomes, family functioning, and social participation. Although numerous studies have examined factors associated with aggression in ASD, findings remain inconsistent, limiting efforts to improve early identification and intervention. This systematic review synthesized current evidence on predictors of aggression in children and adolescents with ASD. The review protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42023416081). A systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library was conducted from database inception to 4 April 2024. Eligible studies were evaluated using the Joanna Briggs Institute Checklist for cross-sectional designs and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for cohort studies, and findings were narratively synthesized. Thirteen studies met inclusion criteria and were of generally satisfactory methodological quality. Across studies, six categories of predictors were identified: demographic, caregiver, core symptom, comorbidity, psychological, and biological factors. Social communication deficits and poor sleep quality showed relatively consistent associations with aggression, although these findings were based on only three and two studies, respectively, whereas evidence for other factors-including age, IQ, caregiver characteristics, and sensory or biological markers-was mixed. Overall, aggression in ASD appears to arise from interacting individual, familial, and contextual influences. These findings highlight the importance of assessing communication skills and sleep problems when evaluating aggression risk and suggest that interventions targeting these domains may reduce aggressive behavior. Future research should employ longitudinal and cross-cultural designs to clarify developmental pathways and strengthen the evidence base for personalized intervention strategies.

papers.title: Efficacy and Safety of Integrated Chinese and Western Medicine for Depression With Anxiety and Somatic Symptoms: A Meta-Analysis.
papers.abstract: ObjectiveSomatic symptoms are often linked with depression and anxiety, making diagnosis difficult and limiting treatment effectiveness. Integrated Traditional Chinese and Western medicine has been studied as a complementary approach; however, its efficacy and safety have not been systematically evaluated. This review and meta-analysis examined the effectiveness and safety of integrated Traditional Chinese and Western medicine in patients diagnosed with depression with or without comorbid anxiety and somatic symptoms.MethodsThis systematic review and meta-analysis followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. English-language studies published from 2014 to 2026 were searched in PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus. Randomized controlled trials comparing integrated therapy with control interventions were included. The primary outcome was depression severity assessed by HAMD scores. Secondary outcomes included anxiety symptoms, somatic symptoms, and adverse events. A random-effects model was used, and heterogeneity was assessed using the I2 statistic.ResultsEleven studies met review criteria. Integrated therapy significantly reduced depression severity compared with the standard Western medicine control condition (MD = -3.95, 95% CI: -4.71 to -3.19; I2 = 59%). Anxiety symptoms were also significantly reduced (MD = -3.95, 95% CI: -4.65 to -3.26; I2 = 50%). Somatic symptoms, including sleep disturbances and pain-related outcomes, improved but were assessed descriptively because of reporting variability. Adverse events were lower or similar in combined treatment groups, indicating a favorable safety profile. Funnel plot analysis suggested minimal publication bias.ConclusionIntegrated Traditional Chinese and Western medicine was associated with greater improvements in depression and anxiety symptoms than the included control interventions, which comprised Western medicine alone, placebo/sham interventions, or usual care, while showing generally good tolerability. However, given the methodological limitations, heterogeneity of comparator conditions, and low certainty of the available evidence, these findings should be interpreted cautiously.

papers.title: A self-organized QTPat-based feature-engineering framework for subject-independent classification of English- and Turkish-associated EEG signals.
papers.abstract: Our primary aim is to develop an automated feature-engineering framework for subject-independent classification of EEG recordings acquired from English-speaking and Turkish-speaking participant cohorts. Drawing inspiration from a quantum tunnel pattern called QTPat, we introduced a novel approach of dynamically generating directed graphs to extract textural features. For our experiments, we utilized an EEG dataset containing 1652 English sentence-EEG pairs and 1600 Turkish sentence-EEG pairs. These signals were recorded from 20 English-speaking and 20 Turkish subjects who were presented with standardized sentences in their respective native languages. During the experiments, the participants were instructed to carefully contemplate each sentence while wearing a mobile brain cap system that acquired 14-channel EEG signals. Our preprocessing pipeline involved subjecting the EEG signals to multiple filtered wavelet packet decompositions, using both 6 Daubechies and 6 symlet wavelet filters. Subsequently, we extracted textural and statistical features employing the QTPat model, along with 20 statistical moments. To enhance discriminative power, we applied neighborhood component analysis and the Chi2-function to select the most relevant features. The k-nearest neighbor classifier was then employed to calculate predictive vectors. To further refine the results, we introduced an iterative hard majority voting scheme, generating additional voted vectors. Finally, we utilized a greedy algorithm to select the best-channel-wise and overall model results. Using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (LOSO CV), the proposed framework achieved 96.37% classification accuracy using four selected EEG channels. These findings demonstrate that the QTPat-based architecture can discriminate the two language-associated EEG cohorts under subject-independent evaluation. However, because language and participant population are coupled in the available dataset, the present results should not be interpreted as definitive evidence of language-specific neural decoding. Further studies using within-subject bilingual experimental designs are required to determine whether the identified EEG patterns specifically reflect language-related neural processing.

papers.title: The impact of creatine on brain functions.
papers.abstract: As an endogenous compound essential for energy homeostasis, creatine holds a fundamental role in the bioenergetics of the brain, an organ with high metabolic requirements. This review provides a synthesis of current knowledge on the impact of creatine on the functions of the central nervous system (CNS). The brain, which is capable of de novo creatine synthesis, demonstrates an increase in its internal concentrations following supplementation; however, this effect is less significant than in muscle tissue and is constrained by the blood-brain barrier, among other factors. The development of effective CNS-targeted dosing strategies remains a subject of ongoing research. An overview of the literature suggests that creatine supplementation may beneficially influence cognitive performance, particularly under conditions of elevated metabolic demand like stress or sleep deprivation, with the potential to enhance memory and mitigate fatigue. Nonetheless, findings from the cited research are inconsistent due to methodological heterogeneity and a common failure to directly measure brain creatine levels. Reports on creatine's antidepressant properties are particularly encouraging, with preclinical and initial clinical studies pointing to its potential utility (e.g., via the mTORC1 pathway) in augmenting mood disorder treatments. Moreover, the authors examine the use of creatine in chronic fatigue syndrome, where evidence supports improvements in physical performance and reductions in pain intensity, although its effect on generalized fatigue remains ambiguous.

papers.title: Effectiveness of Yoga-based guided meditation In Improving the quality of sleep in patients with coronary artery disease: The Yoga Nidra Trial.
papers.abstract: Poor sleep quality has emerged as a risk for coronary artery disease (CAD) and is also associated with poor prognosis and increased mortality. Sleep aids, among CAD patients, lead to increased heart failure, hospitalisation, and mortality. Yoga Nidra, a form of guided meditation, has been shown to improve sleep quality and duration. The aim of the study is to evaluate the adjunctive effect of Yoga Nidra on actigraphy-measured sleep quality parameters, psychological outcomes, and health-related quality of life in patients with CAD. This is a two-arm,1:1 allocation, randomised, controlled, open-label, blinded-endpoint, single-centre trial conducted in a tertiary care hospital between 22-9-2021 and 30-03-2024.144 out of 678 consecutively screened patients with stable CAD and poor sleep quality met the eligibility criteria and were enrolled. Participants were randomised to either a 35-minute, 12-week Yoga Nidra intervention group (n = 72) or a standard care group (n = 72) with sleep hygiene counselling imparted to all patients.The primary outcome was to assess actigraphy-measured sleep efficiency. Secondary outcomes included assessments of actigraphy-derived sleep parameters, ambulatory blood pressure (BP), echocardiographic diastolic function (E/E'), psychological health, and quality-of-life evaluations using validated scales. The Yoga Nidra group exhibited significant improvements in sleep efficiency (82% [76-86] vs. 64% [57-74]; p < 0.05), total sleep time (357 ± 99 min vs. 298 ± 83 min; p < 0.05), reduced sleep latency (15 [11-24] vs. 30 [14-70] min; p < 0.05), and lower wake after sleep onset (48 [28-67] vs. 67 [37-119] min; p < 0.05). Significant improvements were also observed in perceived stress, depression levels, and quality of life. Yoga Nidra is effective in improving sleep quality inpatients with coronary artery disease.Stress, depression, and health-related quality of life also improved with Yoga Nidra.

papers.title: Cannabidiol (CBD) for Pain: A Narrative Review of Evidence to Date.
papers.abstract: Cannabidiol (CBD), the principal non-intoxicating phytocannabinoid of Cannabis sativa, is widely marketed and self-administered for pain relief, yet its regulatory status as an analgesic remains unapproved. This review synthesizes preclinical mechanistic data, human pharmacokinetic data, and clinical trial evidence across major pain conditions in order to summarize the current evidence for, or against, efficacy and safety for pain. A synthesis of published information was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, PubMed Central, Cochrane Library, ScienceDirect, and other databases, integrating findings from systematic reviews, meta-analyses, randomized controlled trials (RCTs), and pharmacology reviews on CBD (independent of combination products where possible) and pain of any etiology. Preclinical and mechanistic data support plausible physical analgesic pathways for CBD, including receptor modulation, indirect enhancement of endocannabinoid tone via fatty-acid-binding-protein (FABP) inhibition, and anti-inflammatory effects. However, translation to clinical benefit has been inconsistent. In the largest meta-analysis of cannabinoids for pain, cannabinoids reduced chronic pain and improved sleep quality, but effect sizes fell below predefined minimally important clinical differences, and cannabinoids showed no benefit for acute or cancer pain, while increasing non-serious adverse events. CBD randomized trials in knee osteoarthritis, fibromyalgia, and acute low back pain have consistently failed to separate from placebo, whereas smaller/lower-quality trials and observational surveys report subjective benefit. Safety data increasingly point to dose-dependent hepatotoxicity risk. Despite strong biological plausibility and considerable consumer use, current high-quality evidence does not support CBD monotherapy as an effective analgesic across most pain conditions studied to date. Safety monitoring, particularly of liver enzymes at higher doses, is warranted.

papers.title: Hybrid sleep-wake states in psychosis: Examining a comprehensive array of unusual sleep and dream experiences in patients with psychosis compared to non-clinical controls.
papers.abstract: Psychosis has been likened to dream-like mentation permeating waking, with hallucinatory experiences, flawed logic, and salience of one's internal world over sensory perception. Some exceptional dream and sleep experiences have been viewed as representing hybrid states between sleep and waking, for example, dreams of falling/flying, dreams of awakening, lucid dreams, sleepwalking, hypnagogic hallucinations, and sleep paralysis. Several of these phenomena have been associated with psychopathological distress in general, and schizotypy and dissociative experiences in particular - dimensional manifestations of core experiences in psychotic disorders. To better understand sleep-wake mechanisms in psychosis, we wished to examine a host of sleep and dream experiences in patients with psychotic disorders. N = 75 patients were compared to n = 72 non-clinical controls on various exceptional sleep/dream experiences, as well as several universal dream themes. The clinical group had poorer sleep quality, and elevated dream phenomena including a general sleep experiences factor (e.g., awakening dreams, falling/flying dreams), lucid dreams, and hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations, even when accounting for sleep quality. Dreams of persecution and grandiosity were elevated in the clinical group, but grandiosity seemed to be confounded by atypical antipsychotic medication use. We exploratorily examined differences between affective and non-affective psychosis but those analyses are limited by sample size. To conclude, researching dreams may shed light on blurred boundaries between wake and sleep in psychosis.

papers.title: De-escalating Therapy in Obstructive Sleep Apnoea After Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonist-Induced Weight Loss: A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Incretin-based therapies now achieve weight reduction of a magnitude previously attainable only through bariatric surgery and have demonstrated substantial reductions in the apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI) in adults with obesity-related obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA). Sleep services are consequently managing growing numbers of patients who undergo rapid, substantial weight loss while established on positive airway pressure (PAP) therapy, and who ask whether that therapy can be stopped. No guideline addresses this question. This narrative review synthesises three literatures that have developed largely in isolation: the relationship between weight change and OSA severity, the efficacy data for glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and dual incretin agonists in OSA, and the experimental PAP withdrawal literature. Across randomised trials and meta-analyses, there is consistent agreement that incretin therapy reduces AHI, body weight and blood pressure, with effect magnitude varying by agent, dose and baseline adiposity. There is, however, material disagreement on three questions directly relevant to de-escalation: whether the effect is wholly weight-mediated, whether AHI reduction translates into reduction in cardiovascular risk, and what proportion of patients achieve genuine disease remission as opposed to severity reduction. Approximately half of participants in the largest trial did not reach a severity threshold at which PAP would ordinarily be considered unnecessary, and withdrawal studies demonstrate recurrence of obstructive events and adverse haemodynamic change within days of stopping therapy. This review proposes a structured, reversible and documented framework for reassessment rather than ad hoc discontinuation and identifies the evidence gaps that must be closed before de-escalation can be considered evidence-based practice.

papers.title: Corollary discharge dysfunction in auditory verbal hallucinations: N100 suppression measured with semi-dry electrodes.
papers.abstract: Corollary discharge dysfunction in patients with auditory verbal hallucinations (AVH) is reflected in failure to attenuate the N100 event-related potential. Previous research has shown mixed findings regarding N100 suppression and hallucination severity, generally using broad symptom scales rather than AVH-specific measures. This study investigated corollary discharge and its relationship with comprehensively characterized auditory hallucinations. Corollary discharge was investigated in 14 patients with persistent auditory hallucinations and 15 healthy controls using an EEG paradigm using semi-dry electrodes where participants self-generated sounds in a "talk" condition and listened to playback in a "listen" condition. N100 suppression was calculated as the peak-amplitude difference (μV) between talk and listen in the 60-150 ms window. Auditory hallucinations were assessed with the Psychotic Symptom Rating Scales Auditory Hallucination Subscale (PSYRATS-AHS). Between-group analysis of the fronto-central ROI (Fz-Cz) showed a statistically non-significant trend toward greater N100 suppression in healthy controls compared to AVH patients (p = 0.095, Cohen's d = 0.64). N100 suppression showed significant negative correlation with hallucination severity in the AVH group (r = -0.54, p = 0.047). Hallucination severity is related to impaired corollary discharge mechanisms, supporting its role as a mechanistic basis for auditory hallucinations. The preliminary correlation with PSYRATS-AHS suggests potential value in using symptom-specific assessment tools in research on auditory hallucinations, warranting replication in larger samples.

papers.title: Normative data of laser evoked potentials using Nd:YAP laser.
papers.abstract: To establish a robust multi-centre normative database for Nd:YAP laser-evoked potentials (LEPs) across distal and proximal stimulation sites, and to quantify the impact of laser spot size (energy density) and demographic factors on LEP parameters. One hundred nine healthy adults (57 females) were recruited from three centres (Geneva, Lyon, Saint-Etienne). Nd:YAP laser pulses were delivered with a 3-mm beam (Centre 1) or 4-mm beam (Centres 2-3). LEPs were recorded from standard EEG sites (including Fz/Cz/Pz and contralateral temporal leads). Stimulation sites included hand dorsum (n = 109), foot dorsum (n = 80), thigh and upper neck (both n = 43). N1, N2, and P2 latencies and amplitudes were measured and normal limits estimated as mean ± 99.9% confidence interval. ANCOVA (age-corrected) tested spot-size effects; repeated-measures ANOVA tested site effects; correlations assessed age/height associations. The vertex N2-P2 complex was consistently recorded across centres and sites (100% for hand, thigh, neck; ∼97% for foot). N1 detection was less consistent, particularly with larger spot size and at the foot. Smaller spot size (higher energy density) yielded shorter N2/P2 latencies and larger N2-P2 amplitudes for hand stimulation, and shorter P2 latency for foot stimulation. Sex and height showed no significant effects. Increasing age was associated with longer N2/P2 latencies and reduced N2-P2 amplitudes for distal sites, with minimal age effects at proximal sites. This study provides the most comprehensive Nd:YAP LEP normative dataset to date, including distal and proximal sites and spot-size-specific reference limits. These data support standardized, high-specificity clinical interpretation of LEPs for assessing small-fibre and spinothalamic pathway dysfunction.

papers.title: Selective mGlu1 Receptor Activation Restores Cortical Inhibitory Tone and Improves Cognitive Performance in a Subchronic Phencyclidine NMDA Hypofunction Model.
papers.abstract: Deficits in prefrontal cortex (PFC) inhibitory transmission are thought to underlie the cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia that remain untreated by current pharmacotherapies. The metabotropic glutamate 1 (mGlu1) receptor, a subtype of the mGlu receptor family, is a promising therapeutic target because its activation enhances inhibitory transmission in the PFC through the excitation of somatostatin-expressing GABAergic (gamma-aminobutyric acidergic) interneurons (SST-INs). We used a subchronic phencyclidine (PCP) NMDA receptor antagonist mouse model, mGlu1 positive allosteric modulators (PAMs), and mice with selective deletion of mGlu1 receptors from SST-INs to examine the cell type-specific role of mGlu1 signaling in cortical inhibition and cognition. We used ex vivo whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology to assess inhibitory transmission in the PFC, and cognitive performance was evaluated using tests of working memory and novel object recognition. Subchronic PCP treatment impaired inhibitory synaptic transmission in the PFC, particularly onto layer V pyramidal neurons projecting to the nucleus accumbens. Pharmacological activation of mGlu1 restored inhibitory drive and reversed PCP-induced deficits in working memory and novel object recognition. Importantly, selective deletion of mGlu1 receptors from SST-INs abolished the ability of mGlu1 activation to restore cortical inhibition and cognitive function, demonstrating that these receptors are required for the therapeutic effects of mGlu1 PAMs. These findings identify SST-IN-expressed mGlu1 receptors as critical regulators of prefrontal cortical inhibition and cognition. Positive allosteric modulation of mGlu1 represents a promising therapeutic strategy for treating cognitive deficits associated with schizophrenia by restoring inhibitory circuit function.

papers.title: Prevalence of night eating syndrome and associated factors among students at Kolej MARA Kuala Nerang: A cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Night eating syndrome (NES) is an eating disorder characterised by recurrent episodes of night eating, morning anorexia and insomnia. This study aimed to determine the prevalence and association of NES with depression, anxiety, stress, sleep quality and eating disorders among students in Kolej MARA Kuala Nerang (KMKN). A cross-sectional study was conducted on 426 students in KMKN. The calculated minimum sample size was 119. A universal sampling method was used, and data on sociodemographic characteristics, NES, depression, anxiety, stress, sleep quality and eating disorders were collected through online self-reported validated questionnaires including the Night Eating Questionnaire; Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale-21; Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index; and Eating Attitudes Test- 26. Data were analysed using IBM SPSS version 22. The chi-square test was used to evaluate the association of NES with sociodemographic characteristics and other factors (P<0.05). A total of 275 students responded (men: 55.6%, women: 44.4%), with 50.9% studying at the Foundation of Science and 49.1% at the Foundation of Science and Technology (FIST). The majority had mild-to-severe depression (56.4%) and anxiety (65.5%); 26.2% were stressed, and 10.2% engaged in NES. NES was not significantly associated with sex, age, monthly pocket money or body mass index. A significant number of students with NES were from the FIST (P=0.036). The factors significantly related to NES were depression (P=0.003), anxiety (P=0.021), stress (P<0.001), poor sleep quality (P=0.001) and risk of eating disorders (P=0.003). NES should be screened among at-risk college students to ensure they receive appropriate treatment.

papers.title: Acute Psychosis and Dissociative Syndrome Following Binge Recreational Nitrous Oxide Use: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Recreational nitrous oxide (N2O) inhalation is increasingly prevalent among young adults, but acute psychiatric presentations following short-term binge exposure remain poorly characterized. We report a case of a female in her early 20s with no prior history of psychotic illness who developed an acute psychotic and dissociative syndrome over three days at an outdoor music festival. Her presentation followed heavy recreational N2O and 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) exposure combined with sleep deprivation. On admission, she exhibited profound disorientation, inability to recognize close family members, polymorphic delusions, passivity phenomena, and auditory and olfactory hallucinations, requiring involuntary psychiatric hospitalization. Diagnostic workup revealed normal brain and cervical spine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and a normal electroencephalogram (EEG) without epileptiform activity or slowing. Serum homocysteine was moderately elevated (25.2 µmol/L) alongside a low-normal vitamin B12 concentration (270 pg/mL), consistent with N2O-induced functional cobalamin deficiency; both markers normalized following parenteral vitamin B12 and oral folic acid supplementation. During inpatient stay, treatment with risperidone was followed by progressive neutropenia, which fully resolved after cross-titration to aripiprazole. She gradually regained full insight, was discharged on day 12, and remained free of psychotic symptoms at her three-week outpatient review. This case suggests that short-term binge N2O exposure, together with MDMA and sleep deprivation, may contribute to severe neuropsychiatric presentations without chronic use; it illustrates the value of measuring homocysteine rather than relying solely on serum B12 levels; and highlights potential hematological adverse effects during antipsychotic initiation.

papers.title: Laser-Based Rejuvenation of the Upper Airway: A Novel Non-Surgical Approach to Habitual Snoring.
papers.abstract: Introduction: This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of Erbium-Doped Yttrium Aluminium Garnet (Er: YAG, 2940 nm), combined with a long-pulse Nd: YAG laser, in mitigating habitual snoring. Methods: Thirty patients participated in the single-arm prospective study, receiving approximately 20,000 pulses of the Er: YAG laser directed at the target sites using a patterned beam from the PSO3X handpiece in Long Pulse (LP) mode, followed by long-pulse Nd: YAG irradiation of the submental and lateral neck region. Treatments were administered on days 0, 15, and 45. The treatment response was evaluated through subjective methods, including the Snore Outcomes Survey (SOS) and the Spouse/Bed Partner Survey (SBPS). Anatomical enhancement was assessed using the Mallampati classification before each session and nine months subsequent to the final session. Results: The mean Mallampati class decreased from 3.50±0.68 to 2.43±0.73. Statistically significant alterations were observed in the SOS and SBPS scores, which increased from 47.10±11.34 to 66.22±11.18 and from 44.38±16.22 to 63.11±14.64, respectively. Older age showed a borderline correlation with the Mallampati class, whereas weight and BMI did not; patients with lower baseline SOS scores tended to improve more. Conclusion: In this single-arm pilot study, the combined Er: YAG and Nd: YAG protocol was well tolerated and was associated with improvements in habitual snoring; controlled trials are required to confirm its efficacy in the early management of snoring.
papers.journal: Journal of lasers in medical sciences

papers.title: Astrocyte molecular rhythm disruption in nucleus accumbens promotes increased binge-like drinking in mice.
papers.abstract: Alcohol misuse is a leading cause of preventable death worldwide. Chronic alcohol is associated with disrupted circadian rhythms, yet molecular mechanisms linking circadian rhythm dysregulation and alcohol consumption are poorly understood. Current FDA-approved treatments for alcohol use disorder (AUD) do not target molecular rhythms or sleep-wake cycles. Mammalian circadian rhythms are regulated by transcription-translation feedback loops that regulate expression of 'clock genes' (e.g., Arntl encoding for BMAL1). Both human and rodent studies demonstrate associations between clock gene variants and changes in reward-seeking behavior. Evidence suggests astrocytes, non-neuronal brain cells with cell-autonomous rhythms, may regulate both circadian rhythms and reward. In the nucleus accumbens (NAc), a region responsible for modulating alcohol- and reward-related behavior, over 43% of the astrocyte transcriptome is expressed rhythmically. However, no studies to date have investigated roles of NAc astrocyte rhythmicity in regulating alcohol drinking. We used AAV8-Gfap-Cre to functionally ablate molecular rhythms in NAc astrocytes of BMAL1 floxed mice. Two-bottle choice (2BC), drinking-in-the-light (DIL), and drinking-in-the-dark (DID) assessed alcohol drinking. Behavioral assays included locomotor response to novelty, sucrose preference, and social interaction. Disrupting molecular clock function in NAc astrocytes increased binge-like drinking during both DIL and DID paradigms ( d = 1.44), but not with any other drinking paradigm or behavior. This study carves out a unique role for astrocytes in controlling the temporal organization of reward circuitry and susceptibility to binge-drinking. Future studies will investigate clock-controlled astrocyte mechanisms, such as glutamate uptake and ATP release, that may underlie binge-like drinking behavior.

papers.title: The effectiveness of sound-based interventions on promoting sleep quality in hospitalized patients: A systematic review.
papers.abstract: Sleep quality strongly affects hospitalized patients' recovery, yet pain, anxiety, and environmental factors such as noise and light frequently disrupt it. Sound-based therapies offer a promising, non-pharmacological approach, but their effectiveness has not been comprehensively synthesized. This systematic review examined fifteen studies (2012-2026, 2024 patients, mostly intensive care settings) evaluating sound-based interventions, including calming music, nature sounds, and white noise, on sleep quality. Intervention duration and timing varied widely, from brief five-minute sessions to continuous overnight administration, and sleep quality was most often measured using validated questionnaires. Despite substantial heterogeneity, sound-based interventions were associated with an overall improvement in sleep quality, although effect sizes varied considerably and several studies showed no significant benefit. These findings support the potential of low-cost, non-pharmacological sound interventions to improve sleep in hospital settings, while underscoring the need for further research to clarify which intervention characteristics drive effectiveness.

papers.title: Convergent and Distinct Transcriptional Signatures in Suicide, Bipolar Disorder, and Major Depressive Disorder.
papers.abstract: Globally, a person dies by suicide every 40 seconds, underscoring a major global public health concern. In the United States, suicide is the second leading cause of death among individuals aged 10-34 years. Suicide is a complex, multifactorial phenomenon influenced by genetic and epigenetic factors and is strongly associated with mood disorders, particularly major depressive disorder (MDD) and bipolar disorder (BD). However, the extent to which their molecular signatures converge or diverge across disorders and brain regions remains incompletely understood. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic literature review of suicide, MDD, and BD transcriptomic studies in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science. Eligible studies used human postmortem brain tissue, reported a complete genome-wide transcriptomic list of differentially expressed genes (DEG), and compared suicide decedents with psychiatric non-suicide individuals diagnosed with the same underlying disorder. Regarding BD, studies comparing affected individuals to unaffected controls were included. Single-cell and peripheral-blood studies were excluded because unavailable for suicide. Curated suicide and BD DEG datasets were integrated with a published bulk transcriptomic dataset of MDD. We identified both shared and disease-specific molecular signatures across suicide, BD, and MDD, and identified DEGs shared across brain regions and those that were region-specific. A total of 276 genes were shared across all three conditions, implicating cellular stress, hypoxia (VEGFA, ADM, NDRG1, DDIT4), immune and inflammatory signaling through TNFα/NF-κB (IL1B, ICAM1, NFE2L2) and IL6-JAK-STAT3 pathways (STAT3, SOCS3, IL1R1m OSMR), complement activation (CIR, SERPiNA1, LGALS3), extracellular matrix remodeling (COL4A1, SERPINH1, PLOD2), and unfolded protein response (BAG3, WFS1, MTHFD2). Suicide-associated DEGs were prominently downregulated, and involved metal-ion homeostasis, stress responses, synaptic regulation, and circadian pathways, whereas BD showed downregulation in synaptic and vesicle-related processes alongside region-specific metabolic dysregulation. MDD exhibited changes in RNA processing, ribosomal function, and protein synthesis. Genetic integration revealed that 133 genes shared between BD and MDD had gene variants associated with the corresponding condition per GWAS. Transcription factor analysis identified 20 regulatory factors with altered activity across all three conditions despite differences in their predicted downstream targets. Overall, these findings suggest that suicide, MDD, and BD share aspects of their molecular and regulatory pathophysiology while exhibiting distinct patterns, including in a region-specific manner.

papers.title: Channelrhodopsin ion selectivity determines mechanisms and efficacy of optogenetic defibrillation in human atria and ventricles.
papers.abstract: Cardiac re-entrant arrhythmias are a major cause of sudden cardiac death. Optogenetic defibrillation has emerged as a promising anti-arrhythmic strategy based on photoactivation of channelrhodopsins, yet the efficacy and potential adverse consequences of activating different classes of light-gated ion channels have not been systematically evaluated. Previous studies assessed either cation (e.g. ChR2) or anion (e.g. GtACR1) non-selective channels, both of which depolarize resting cardiomyocytes. Recently identified light-gated K+ channels (e.g. WiChR) suppress cardiomyocyte activity while maintaining the membrane potential near its resting state, but their defibrillation potential remains unexplored. We used computational simulations to compare ChR2, GtACR1 and WiChR. Single-cell simulations showed that ChR2 and GtACR1 markedly increased diastolic intracellular Ca2+ (by 42.6% and 52.6%, respectively), whereas WiChR induced only minimal changes (by 4.0%), suggesting lower pro-arrhythmogenic risk. WiChR, however, slightly increased intracellular Na+ (by 15.1% vs. 0.1% and 3.4% for ChR2 and GtACR1), consistent with the residual Na+ permeability of currently available K+-conducting channelrhodopsins. Simulations in human ventricles and atria showed that GtACR1 most effectively terminated re-entrant arrhythmias at low light intensities, whereas WiChR achieved comparable efficacy at ≥5 mW/mm2. Complementary tissue-scale simulations revealed that defibrillation occurs through depolarization within the excitable gap followed by fast Na+ channel inactivation (ChR2 and partly GtACR1), or through reduced membrane resistance at sufficiently high light intensities (large-conductance channels GtACR1 and WiChR). Overall, we demonstrate that channelrhodopsin ion selectivity is a key determinant of both optogenetic defibrillation efficacy and its underlying mechanisms. TRANSLATIONAL PERSPECTIVE: Re-entrant arrhythmias are a leading cause of sudden cardiac death. Standard therapies, including the activation of implantable cardioverter-defibrillators, carry burdens such as pain and myocardial injury. Optogenetic defibrillation has been suggested as a potentially gentler alternative, replacing high-voltage electrical shocks by photoactivation of light-gated ion channels expressed in cardiac cells. Determining which light-gated ion channel optimally balances efficacy and adverse effects on cardiac electrophysiology is critical for clinical translation. We addressed this question using computational simulations and validation experiments in zebrafish hearts. We identify ion selectivity as a key determinant of both the success rate for arrhythmia termination and the underlying mechanisms: non-selective cation- and anion-conducting channels terminate re-entry efficiently while promoting intracellular Ca2+ accumulation, a plausible substrate for pro-arrhythmic side effects that could undermine therapeutic safety. K+-conducting channels largely avoid this pro-arrhythmic risk by holding cardiomyocytes near their resting potential, albeit at the cost of requiring transmural illumination, while also causing mild Na+ accumulation attributable to residual Na+ permeability. Together, these trade-offs define clear clinical implications: K+-conducting channels may provide the safest option for optogenetic defibrillation, particularly once variants with further enhanced K+ selectivity and red-shifted activation spectra for improved operation within blood-perfused myocardium become available. KEY POINTS: We use computational simulations to compare cation non-selective (ChR2), anion non-selective (GtACR1) and K+-selective (WiChR) channelrhodopsins for optogenetic termination of re-entrant arrhythmia. Single-cardiomyocyte simulations suggest that ChR2 and GtACR1 activation can cause progressive accumulation of intracellular Ca2+, which is minimized when using WiChR. Intracellular microelectrode recordings from hearts of transgenic adult zebrafish validate the simulated voltage dynamics seen with ChR2, GtACR1 or WiChR activation. Simulations of human left ventricles and atria indicate that GtACR1 is most effective in terminating re-entrant arrhythmia at low light intensities, whereas WiChR becomes similarly effective at higher intensities. Tissue-scale simulations indicate distinct defibrillation mechanisms: excitable gap extinction by de novo action potential initiation followed by inactivation of fast Na+ channels for depolarizing channelrhodopsins (ChR2, GtACR1), and reduction in membrane resistance for the large-conductance channels (GtACR1, WiChR), effectively clamping the membrane potential at each channel's reversal potential at high light levels.

papers.title: Differential Cerebral Perfusion Patterns Across Migraine Phenotypes: An Exploratory ASL MRI Study.
papers.abstract: This study aims to characterize cerebral blood flow (CBF) alterations across migraine phenotypes and determine whether perfusion measures provide additional information for phenotype differentiation. The final cohort comprised 143 patients with migraine and 49 healthy controls who underwent three-dimensional pseudo-continuous arterial spin labeling (ASL) MRI. Voxel-wise analyses of normalized CBF (nCBF) were performed to identify phenotype-related perfusion alterations. Sensitivity analyses repeated the voxel-wise comparisons with phenotype-appropriate clinical covariates. Exploratory correlation analyses examined associations between regional perfusion and clinical characteristics. Logistic regression was further used to assess whether perfusion measures provided additional information for differentiating migraine with aura (MA) from migraine without aura (MO). Compared with healthy controls, migraine patients with depressive symptoms showed reduced nCBF in a right hippocampus-parahippocampal cluster (Cluster 1) in the primary voxel-wise analysis; however, this finding did not survive additional adjustment for sleep quality. Lower Cluster 1 nCBF was associated with greater headache frequency. Compared with MO, patients with MA showed increased nCBF in a right cerebellar-occipitotemporal cluster peaking in the right cerebellar Crus I (Cluster 2), and this difference remained significant after additional adjustment for sleep quality, medication-overuse headache status, and preventive medication exposure. Within the MA group, higher Cluster 2 nCBF was associated with greater headache intensity. In exploratory logistic regression analysis, the combined clinical-imaging model showed a higher apparent area under the curve (AUC) than the clinical model alone. Clinically relevant migraine phenotypes showed distinct patterns of regional cerebral perfusion. These findings highlight the importance of considering clinical heterogeneity in migraine neuroimaging and suggest that ASL-derived perfusion measures may provide complementary biological information for phenotype characterization, particularly with respect to aura status.

papers.title: Gut microbiome composition and cardiometabolic risk among healthcare workers: findings from the EXPONIT study.
papers.abstract: The gut microbiome plays an important role in metabolic regulation and has been linked to cardiometabolic disorders. Circadian-related factors (night shift work, sleep quality, chronotype) may influence gut microbiome characteristics and cardiometabolic health. We aimed to investigate the associations between gut microbiome diversity and composition and cardiometabolic outcomes, and evaluate whether these associations differ by work schedule, sleep quality, and chronotype. Fecal samples were taken on a working day, and gut microbiota composition was assessed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Anthropometric measures (body mass index,waist-to-hip ratio, systolic and diastolic blood pressure) and blood samples (metabolic biomarkers), were obtained during study visits. Associations between microbial composition and cardiometabolic outcomes were examined using robust linear and logistic regression models. Potential interactions with shift work status, sleep quality, and chronotype were also explored. Overall, alpha diversity was not significantly associated with cardiometabolic markers. However, overall gut microbiome composition (beta diversity) was associated with excess body weight (PERMANOVA p = 0.01, R2 = 0.7%). In addition, specific genera were associated with anthropometric markers: greater relative abundance of Lachnospiraceae-unclassified-genus-008 was associated with a higher body mass index; and increased relative abundance of Escherichia/Shigella and lower relative abundance of Alistipes were associated with higher waist-to-hip ratio. No associations were found between beta diversity or taxonomic composition and metabolic biomarkers. Specific gut microbial profiles may be associated with cardiometabolic markers, particularly obesity-related traits. Future longitudinal studies are needed to clarify the directionality and underlying mechanisms of these associations.
papers.journal: Nutrition, metabolism, and cardiovascular diseases : NMCD

papers.title: Interplay of action-based prediction and top-down attention: EEG evidence for joint modulation of late perceptual processing.
papers.abstract: Voluntary action shapes our perception through sensory predictions of its consequences. These predictions are thought to inhibit perceptual processing of predicted outcomes, leading to sensory attenuation. However, some studies have reported findings that contrast with this effect, suggesting that the influence of predictions may reflect, or interact with, attentional processes. Here, we investigated the interplay of action-based prediction and top-down attention on early and late perceptual processing, with prediction and attention referring to the likelihood of a sensory event and its behavioral relevance, respectively. Electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded while participants viewed two sequential gratings. The orientation of the first was either predicted and self-generated or unpredicted and externally generated. Participants judged the tilt direction of the second grating relative to the first but responded only when the grating appeared in a task-relevant color. EEG analyses revealed no modulation of early visual potentials (N1a), but modulations at later processing stages. Specifically, the P3b exhibited reduced amplitude for predicted compared to unpredicted stimuli, but only when they were task-relevant, whereas task-relevance enhanced the P3b only for unpredicted stimuli. Interestingly, multivariate pattern analysis showed significant temporal clusters for decoding the grating's orientation exclusively for predicted and task-relevant stimuli, although decoding performance did not significantly differ between conditions. Furthermore, predicted and task-relevant stimuli elicited faster behavioral responses, with prediction-related P3b latency differences correlating with reaction-time differences. Overall, converging findings from the P3b, multivariate, time-frequency and behavioral analyses provide suggestive evidence that top-down attention and action-based prediction may jointly facilitate late perceptual and decision-related processing.

papers.title: SIFamide Signaling regulates energy mobilization during phototactic behavior in the Asian Citrus psyllid, Diaphorina citri.
papers.abstract: Phototactic behavior is an energy-intensive visually guided behavior critical for insect survival and dispersal. The central neuromodulatory mechanisms underlying this oriented response remain poorly understood, particularly with respect to peptidergic regulation. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted a study on the Asian citrus psyllid, Diaphorina citri, a vector of citrus huanglongbing, whose adults exhibit robust positive phototaxis. The SIFamide (SIFa) neuropeptide (DcSIFa) and its cognate receptor (DcSIFaR) were identified, both of which showed the highest expression levels in the head. Immunofluorescence analysis revealed two pairs of SIFa-producing neurons in the pars intercerebralis with widespread brain-wide arborizations. Expression of both genes was dynamically upregulated in phototactic individuals. RNAi-mediated knockdown of either gene substantially reduced phototactic behavior, downregulated energy metabolism genes, disrupted mitochondrial respiratory function, and altered nitrogen metabolism and circadian rhythm. Physiologically, gene silencing led to reduced heart rate, lower oxygen consumption, and decreased production of adenosine triphosphate and citric acid. These findings demonstrate that SIFamide signaling acts as a central neuromodulatory hub regulating energy mobilization during phototactic behavior in D. citri, and indicate that DcSIFa or DcSIFaR may serve as promising candidate targets for pest control strategies.

papers.title: Maternal piromelatine treatment is associated with attenuated behavioral alterations and sex-specific changes in hippocampal pCREB/BDNF signaling in adult offspring following prenatal constant-light exposure.
papers.abstract: Maternal exposure to constant light during pregnancy (CLE) is associated with disrupted circadian organization and persistent behavioral alterations in adult offspring. This study examined behavioural performance and 24-hour locomotor activity patterns, as well as hippocampal pCREB and BDNF levels, in adult male and female offspring following prenatal CLE and maternal treatment with piromelatine (pir), which acts as an agonist at melatonin MT1/MT2 and serotonin 5-HT1A/5-HT1D receptors. Pregnant Wistar rats under light-dark regime received vehicle (veh), whereas dams exposed to CLE received vehicle (LL-veh), pir (10mg/kg), or melatonin. Compared to the LL-veh groups, offspring from pir-treated dams exhibited reduced anxiety- and depression-like responses and improved working memory in both sexes. Individual-subject cosinor analysis revealed heterogeneous 24-hour locomotor rhythmicity within and between groups. No significant treatment-group effect was detected for MESOR or amplitude, and the descriptive acrophase patterns did not provide evidence of treatment-induced restoration or normalization of circadian organization. Maternal pir treatment was associated with higher hippocampal pCREB and BDNF levels in male, but not female offspring relative to the LL-veh group. While the behavioral and molecular differences occurred concurrently in males, these findings do not prove that pCREB/BDNF signaling mediated the behavioral outcomes. Furthermore, the study cannot distinguish the direct developmental effects of maternal pir exposure from those mediated through maternal or offspring circadian rhythm. Therefore, the findings should be interpreted as long-term behavioral and sex-specific molecular differences associated with maternal pir treatment rather than as evidence of circadian-independent antidepressant, anxiolytic, cognitive-enhancing, or BDNF-enhancing actions.

papers.title: A Reproducible Safety Assessment Model for Concurrent Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation with Implanted Intracranial Electroencephalography Electrodes.
papers.abstract: Concurrent transcranial magnetic stimulation and intracranial EEG (TMS-sEEG) offers a powerful approach for interrogating human brain circuits with high spatiotemporal resolution. However, standardized safety testing procedures for TMS in the presence of implanted electrodes are lacking. To establish and validate a reproducible methodological framework for assessing TMS safety with sEEG hardware, addressing potential risks of electrode displacement, heating, and secondary current induction. A conductive agarose phantom implanted with clinical-grade platinum sEEG electrodes was exposed to single-pulse TMS (0.4 Hz), repetitive TMS (1-50 Hz), and intermittent theta burst stimulation. Electrode displacement was quantified via high-speed video and motion tracking. Temperature changes were measured with fiber-optic thermal probes positioned at stimulated electrode contacts. Induced voltages were recorded using an oscilloscope and intracranial EEG hardware, and secondary current and charge density were calculated from oscilloscope outputs and impedance measurements. sEEG lead displacement remained micrometer-scale across stimulation conditions, with a maximum transient displacement of 10.99 μm and a maximum 1-s mean displacement from the pre-TMS position of 16.27 μm. Temperature changes remained well within the 2°C safety threshold across all tested conditions; in the primary temperature series, the maximum observed increase was 0.073°C. Induced voltages and charge densities remained below established safety limits, exhibiting consistent exponential decay with increasing distance from the coil. All stimulation conditions, including those exceeding typical clinical ranges, remained well within safety margins. Under the tested conditions in a controlled phantom environment, TMS exposure produced micrometer-scale transient and longer-timescale displacement, temperature changes within established safety thresholds, and charge densities within established safety thresholds. This validated methodological pipeline provides a standardized framework for future safety experiments involving TMS and implanted devices and supports continued development of TMS-sEEG as a tool for studying human brain circuitry and neuromodulation.

papers.title: Altered resting-state EEG microstate dynamics are associated with auditory hallucinations in patients with major depressive disorder.
papers.abstract: Auditory hallucination experiences are an understudied but clinically significant feature of major depressive disorder (MDD). Although EEG microstate abnormalities have been reported in MDD, their relationship with auditory hallucination experiences remains unclear. This study investigated resting-state EEG microstate dynamics associated with auditory hallucination experiences in first-episode MDD. A total of 182 first-episode patients with MDD and 95 healthy controls underwent resting-state EEG recordings. Patients were classified according to lifetime history of auditory hallucination experiences into those with (AH+, n = 42) and without (AH-, n = 140) such experiences. Patients were either psychotropic medication-naïve or minimally medicated (<2 weeks of cumulative exposure). Microstate parameters were compared among groups. ANCOVA and hierarchical binary logistic regression were performed to examine associations with auditory hallucination experiences. Only microstate C occurrence was significantly higher in the AH+ group than in both the AH- and healthy control groups after multiple-comparison correction. This difference remained significant after adjustment for age, sex, education, and depression severity. Hierarchical logistic regression showed that higher microstate C occurrence was independently associated with auditory hallucination experiences (OR = 1.773, 95% CI: 1.211-2.595, p = 0.003), but not with hallucination severity. Its discriminatory ability was modest (AUC = 0.614, 95% CI: 0.516-0.711). In first-episode MDD, a lifetime history of auditory hallucination experiences was associated with increased microstate C occurrence. This finding suggests that altered microstate C dynamics may represent an electrophysiological correlate of auditory hallucination experiences, warranting further investigation.

papers.title: Multidimensional Clinical Benefits of Cinnamon Leaf Oil Inhalation in Primary and Metastatic Brain Tumor Patients During Winter: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: To evaluate the multidimensional efficacy of 12‑week cinnamon leaf oil (CLO) inhalation as a seasonal adjuvant supportive‑care intervention for alleviating winter‑exacerbated non‑motor symptom burden and improving mood disorders, sleep quality, refractory fatigue, and functional independence in patients with primary and metastatic brain tumors. This randomized, controlled clinical trial enrolled 328 patients diagnosed with primary or metastatic brain tumors, randomly assigned at a 1:1 ratio to intervention group (standard antitumor care plus 12‑week undiluted CLO inhalation, 2h/day, 5 days/week, n=165) or control group (standard care plus distilled‑water‑vapor sham‑aromatherapy control, n=163). Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics were descriptively summarized for both groups. The primary outcome was the change in HAM-D total score from baseline to week 12. Secondary outcome indicators included changes in anxiety (HAM‑A), sleep quality (PSQI), physical/mental fatigue (FS-14), and activities of daily living (ADL-BI). Integrated multidimensional outcome profiling was further performed to examine changes across six clinical domains. Twelve weeks of CLO inhalation was associated with improvements across the assessed outcome measures, whereas the control group receiving only standard care showed minimal clinical changes. The intervention group showed reductions in emotional symptoms, with HAM‑A scores decreasing from 17.65±4.48 to 12.25±4.51 (p<0.001) and HAM‑D scores declining from 22.10±5.41 to 13.68±2.71 (p<0.001). Improvements in sleep quality were observed, with PSQI total scores dropping from 12.18±3.05 to 5.25±1.86 (p<0.01). Additionally, the CLO group showed changes in functional independence, with ADL‑BI total scores increasing from 63.60±14.16 to 74.88±11.33 (p<0.01). In terms of fatigue relief, the proportions of patients with severe physical and mental fatigue decreased by 46% and 76%, respectively (p<0.01). Multidimensional profiling indicated favourable changes for CLO inhalation across sleep, anxiety, depression, physical fatigue remission, mental fatigue remission and daily function. Only mild Grade 1 transient mucosal irritation adverse events occurred in the intervention group with low incidence; no severe adverse reactions or trial withdrawal were observed. Findings from this single‑centre trial suggest that 12‑week standardized CLO inhalation may represent a tolerable non‑pharmacological adjuvant approach for brain tumour patients. It was associated with reductions in winter‑exacerbated anxiety, depression, sleep disturbance, and refractory fatigue, as well as improvements in patients' functional independence. Observations of multi‑domain symptom changes warrant further clinical investigation to evaluate its utility within neuro‑oncological supportive‑care practice and patients' long‑term quality‑of‑life outcomes.

papers.title: Non-coding RNA levels integrating analysis revealed the salt and drought stress response mechanism of miR395e-PvUXS1 pathway in switchgrass.
papers.abstract: Soil salinization and drought are major constraints on global agricultural production, yet the shared molecular mechanisms by which forage crops respond to these stresses remain incompletedly understood. Identifying candidate genes with potential value for stress-resilient breeding is therefore an important research objective. Switchgrass (Panicum virgatum L.) is a perennial forage and bioenergy crop with adaptation to saline, semi-arid, and drought-prone environments. In this study, RNA sequencing was used to investate the responses of switchgrass to two salt-stress conditions (300mM NaCl treatment and 10‰ soil salinity). Differentially expressed (DE) mRNAs shared by the two salt-stress conditions were significantly enriched in pathways related to carbon metabolism and carbon fixation in photosynthetic organisms. Whole-transcriptome RNA sequencing further identified DE mRNAs, microRNAs (miRNAs), long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), and circular RNAs (circRNAs) associated with salt and drought responses. Competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) network analysis identified four KEGG pathways commonly enriched under salt and drought stress: photosynthesis, circadian rhythm in plants, ribosome biogenesis in eukaryotes, and aminoacyl-tRNA biosynthesis. Notably, the UDP-glucuronic acid decarboxylase gene PvUXS1 (Pavir.5NG221800) involved in amino sugar and nucleotide sugar metabolism, was identified as target of miR395e. Salt and drought stress reduced miR395e expression while increasing PvUXS1 expression, and further validation showed that miR395e negatively regulates PvUXS1. Together, these results identify a previously uncharacterized miR395e-PvUXS1 regulatory pathway and provide a potential molecular target for improving stress tolerance in switchgrass.
papers.journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology

papers.title: Social appearance anxiety and adult picky eating: Associations with sleep quality, depressive symptoms, and body mass index.
papers.abstract: Although adult picky eating has traditionally received limited attention, it is now recognized as a persistent eating behaviour with important psychosocial implications. However, its associations with sleep quality, depressive symptoms, body mass index (BMI), and social appearance anxiety remain insufficiently investigated, especially in non-Western settings. This study explored the relationships between adult picky eating and these psychological and health-related variables among Turkish adults. A cross-sectional study was conducted with 386 adults aged 18 years and older in Türkiye using an online snowball sampling method. Participants completed the Adult Picky Eating Questionnaire (APEQ), the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), and the Social Appearance Anxiety Scale (SAAS). Sociodemographic information and BMI were also obtained. Between-group comparisons were performed using the Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis tests. Spearman's rank correlation and multiple linear regression analyses were used to examine the associations and independent correlates of picky eating. In multivariable linear regression analysis, social appearance anxiety showed a modest, independent positive association with picky eating (B = 0.103, β = 0.201, p < 0.001), whereas BMI exhibited a weak inverse association (B = -0.176, β = -0.121, p = 0.033). Depressive symptoms and sleep quality were not independently associated with total picky eating scores. The overall model explained 7.7% of the variance. Exploratory bivariate correlations indicated a modest positive relationship between social appearance anxiety and total APEQ scores (ρ = 0.264, p < 0.001) with similar patterns observed across subscales, while associations involving depressive symptoms and sleep quality were largely weak or non-significant. In this adult sample, picky eating showed a modest positive association with social appearance anxiety and a weak inverse association with body mass index, whereas depressive symptoms and overall sleep quality were not independently associated. These observational findings suggest that appearance-related concerns may be relevant to individual variations in adult picky eating. However, the cross-sectional design, the low explanatory power of the multivariable model (R2 = 0.077), and the modest internal consistency of the APEQ require cautious interpretation and preclude causal, physiological, or clinical inferences. Future prospective studies incorporating comprehensive assessments of sensory sensitivity, food neophobia, body image, and dietary intake are needed to clarify the temporal and contextual factors associated with adult picky eating.

papers.title: Multidimensional sleep health and suicide risk in older depressed adults.
papers.abstract: A variety of sleep dimensions are associated with suicidal thoughts and behavior in late life. However, sleep is not experienced as a singular dimension. This study examined associations of multidimensional sleep health with life-time suicide attempt and current suicidal desire in older depressed adults. Participants (N = 72, mean age: 60.5 ± 5.6 years; 60% women; 22% nonwhite; with 32 past suicide attempters and 40 non-attempters) completed a 3-week protocol involving ecological momentary assessment and wrist actigraphy. Multidimensional sleep health was quantified using actigraphic measures of sleep efficiency, timing, duration, and regularity, and sleep diary measures of satisfaction. Each component was dichotomized and then summed to create a composite score (0-6); higher values indicated worse sleep health. Participants completed weekly clinical assessments of suicidal ideation. Separate regression models tested associations of multidimensional sleep health and its individual components with current suicidal desire and life-time suicide attempt adjusting for covariates. A 1-point change in worse multidimensional sleep health was associated with 2.0 times greater odds of current suicidal ideation (OR: 1.990; 95% CI: 1.146 - 3.456; p = 0.015). Among its components, greater irregularity of sleep duration and sleep timing were associated with current suicidal desire . After adjusting for depression severity, the association between multidimensional sleep health and suicidal desire was attenuated by 56%. Multidimensional sleep health is associated with current suicidal desire but not lifetime suicide attempt in older depressed adults. Future research should determine whether regularity of sleep duration and timing is an intervention target for reducing current suicidal ideation.

papers.title: Dorsolateral prefrontal TMS-evoked N100 as a neurophysiological correlate of symptom change in adolescent depression.
papers.abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is highly prevalent in adolescence. Up to 30% of patients insufficiently benefit from first-line treatments, underscoring the need for improved treatment strategies and better understanding of pathophysiology. In depression, an imbalance between cortical excitation and inhibition in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), assessed by the TMS-evoked N100 potential, is suggested as one of several contributing neurobiological mechanisms. While elevated N100 amplitudes have been observed in depressed adults and adolescents, its association with symptom change remains insufficiently investigated. In a randomized controlled trial, N = 54 adolescents (38 girls, 16 boys) with MDD received six weeks of whole body vibration training (exercising on a vibrating plate that triggers involuntary muscle contractions through a neurological reflex) or light stretching as add-on treatments to treatment as usual. TMS-EEG was applied before and after the intervention to assess N100 amplitudes over the left and right DLPFC. Depressive symptoms were measured using the Children's Depression Rating Scale-Revised. Changes in N100 amplitudes were analyzed using repeated measures ANOVA. Multiple regression analyses with intervention group as predictor examined associations between changes in N100 amplitudes and depressive symptoms, including sex as moderator and a subsequent girls-only analysis. Across both groups, N100 amplitudes significantly decreased from pre-to post-intervention. No differential effects between interventions were observed. Reductions in right-hemispheric N100 amplitudes were significantly associated with improvements in depressive symptoms. This association reached statistical significance in girls. Our findings support the N100 as a candidate neurophysiological correlate of depressive symptom improvement.

papers.title: Sleep-state transition instability with recurrent multisystem activation: A case-based phenotypic framework.
papers.abstract: The wake-to-sleep transition is a physiologically vulnerable period during which benign and pathologic motor phenomena may emerge. Current sleep nosology recognizes isolated hypnic jerks, propriospinal myoclonus at sleep onset, sleep-related rhythmic movement disorder, and other minor sleep-related motor activities, but these entities may not fully explain patients with persistent, repetitive motor activation recurring across successive attempts to fall asleep. We describe eight representative cases characterized by recurrent motor events centered on sleep onset or early sleep-state transitions, associated sensory and autonomic symptoms, clinically meaningful sleep fragmentation, and absence of a more satisfactory alternative diagnosis. On the basis of these observations, we introduce sleep-state transition instability with recurrent multisystem activation (SSTI-RMA) as a provisional, hypothesis-generating phenotypic construct rather than an established diagnostic entity. The recurring clinical pattern comprises recurrent motor activation during wake-to-sleep or early sleep transitions together with variable sensory, autonomic, cardiovascular, respiratory, or other non-motor manifestations, repetition or clustering of events, difficulty initiating or stabilizing sleep, clinically significant distress or impairment, and absence of a more satisfactory alternative explanation. We conceptualize the SSTI-RMA phenotype as a possible disorder of sleep-state instability rather than as an isolated motor phenomenon, potentially involving impaired coordination among neural, autonomic, and vascular processes during sleep entry. No validated polysomnographic signature, frequency threshold, biomarker, or prevalence estimate is currently available, and the relationship of this phenotype to severe or recurrent sleep starts remains unresolved. SSTI-RMA should therefore be regarded as a descriptive research framework intended to facilitate standardized phenotyping and prospective studies capable of determining whether it represents a distinct entity, part of a continuum of established sleep-onset phenomena, or a heterogeneous phenotype with multiple causes.

papers.title: Distinct daytime sleepiness phenotypes across insomnia symptom dimensions in the Wisconsin sleep cohort.
papers.abstract: Insomnia symptoms are heterogeneous, and it remains unclear whether difficulty initiating sleep (DIS), difficulty maintaining sleep (DMS), operationalized as repeated nighttime awakening, and early morning awakening (EMA) correspond to distinct joint patterns of subjective daytime sleepiness and physiological sleep propensity. We examined these symptom-specific phenotypes and their clinical burden. We analyzed 881 Wisconsin Sleep Cohort participants with complete Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) and Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT) data. Four phenotypes were defined by ESS >10 and MSLT <8 min: Neither, Subjective-only, Objective-only, and Both. DIS, DMS, and EMA were assessed using self-reported questionnaire items and were entered simultaneously in adjusted multinomial logistic regression. Greater DIS severity was associated with lower ESS (β = -0.70, 95% confidence interval (CI) -1.02 to -0.39), longer MSLT latency (β = 0.45 min, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.80), and lower relative risk of Both (relative risk ratio (RRR) = 0.67, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.87). Greater DMS severity was associated with higher ESS (β = 0.43, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.66) and higher relative risk of Both (RRR = 1.30, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.56). EMA was not associated with the overall phenotype distribution. Within frequent DMS, Subjective-only sleepiness was associated with higher depression and trait anxiety after false discovery rate adjustment. DIS and DMS were associated with different daytime sleepiness profiles. Within frequent DMS, subjective sleepiness identified greater psychological burden. The observed associations were generally modest and support considering nocturnal symptom pattern when interpreting daytime sleepiness.

papers.title: Effectiveness of estetrol 15 mg combined with drospirenone 3 mg for symptom control in women with endometriosis: a systematic review.
papers.abstract: To systematically evaluate the effectiveness of estetrol (E4) combined with drospirenone (DRSP) in reducing endometriosis-related symptoms and improving quality of life (QoL). We conducted a systematic review in accordance with Cochrane Collaboration guidelines and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment. A third author resolved disagreements between the reviewers. We conducted a comprehensive search across PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, without language or date restrictions. We included two RCTs and two observational cohorts, encompassing a total of 198 patients. Quantitative synthesis was not feasible for the outcomes due to the limited number of eligible studies and the lack of sufficient comparable data. E4/DRSP demonstrated a significant reduction in pelvic pain compared with placebo, whereas no significant differences were observed when compared with other active hormonal regimens. Treatment with E4/DRSP also was associated with clinically meaningful improvements in dysmenorrhea symptoms. Furthermore, E4/DRSP improved QoL in women with endometriosis, with improvements in sleep quality, patient- and clinician-reported global improvement and overall health status. The findings regarding dyspareunia were inconsistent. The most common adverse effect was intermenstrual bleeding/spotting. Based on the current evidence, E4/DRSP appears to be a promising option for the management of endometriosis-related symptoms, particularly improving pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, and QoL. This systematic review, conducted according to Cochrane and PRISMA guidelines, indicated that E4/DRSP may be effective in reducing endometriosis-associated symptoms, although its superiority over other combined hormonal contraceptives remains uncertain.
papers.journal: European journal of obstetrics, gynecology, and reproductive biology

papers.title: "I'm much more ok with my body just being mine and treating it well": women's experiences of empowerment after completing a holistic health programme.
papers.abstract: Women are often disempowered by dominant discourses that narrowly define health in terms of weight, exercise, and diet. This study explored women's experiences of empowerment after completing Next Level Health (NLH), a holistic health programme that supported women to make small, achievable behaviour change across health domains including physical activity, sleep, nutrition, eating behaviour, self-care, and stress management. Fifty-six women living in New Zealand completed evaluation forms that asked about their experiences of NLH and any outcomes they experienced at programme-end (6 months) and follow-up (12 months). Four themes were identified through reflexive thematic analysis. Women were empowered through (1) embedded health routines, (2) adopting a holistic perspective, (3) health literacy in daily life, and (4) reframing success. Collectively, these themes reveal the expansive and personal ways empowerment was realised and the context sensitivity it required. These findings highlight how women gained greater agency over their health by shifting away from rigid norms towards context-sensitive and self-directed health practices. There is compelling evidence that future health interventions should embed holistic, women-centred approaches, with reflexive practice playing a key role in women's empowerment.

papers.title: Molecular triage and isoform protection safeguard ubiquitin chain editing on DNA.
papers.abstract: In an accompanying study, we identify the RPA-ZUP1 complex as a ubiquitin chain-editing machine that promotes removal of RPA from ssDNA. Because loss of ZUP1 causes pathological RPA trapping on ssDNA, cells must preserve a functional RPA-ZUP1 pool to sustain RPA turnover. How this homeostasis is achieved is unknown. Here, we show that ZUP1 is subject to ubiquitin-dependent fate control. ZUP1 ubiquitination promotes recruitment of p97/VCP and ATXN3, defining a molecular triage pathway that protects ZUP1 from premature proteasomal degradation. Opposing this, the E3 ligases UBR5 and HUWE1 define a degradative branch that limits ZUP1 abundance, with HUWE1 restricting its accumulation on damaged chromatin. We further show that cells express a naturally occurring ZUP1 isoform resistant to efficient ubiquitination and turnover, suggesting that isoform diversity provides a protected pool of chain-editing activity. Together, these findings define a homeostatic system that preserves ZUP1 while limiting its persistence on damaged chromatin.

papers.title: Circadian rhythms and sleep disturbances: a conceptual perspective with implications for autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.
papers.abstract: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is a genetic disorder characterized by cyst formation, kidney enlargement, and extrarenal complications. While the role of genetic mutations in PKD1, PKD2, and other minor genes is well established, the influence of circadian rhythms and sleep disturbances on disease progression remains underexplored. The circadian timing system, coordinated by the central clock in the suprachiasmatic nucleus and synchronized with peripheral clocks in the kidneys, regulates key physiological processes, including glomerular filtration rate (GFR), sodium handling, blood pressure, and hormone secretion. In ADPKD, circadian disruption driven by intrinsic molecular alterations and exacerbated by sleep disorders contributes to sympathetic nervous system activation, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) dysregulation, and elevated vasopressin levels, all of which accelerate cyst growth and hypertension. Mechanistic links also involve the activation of the mTOR pathway, impaired fatty acid oxidation, and altered gut microbiota composition. These disturbances impair kidney function and increase the risk of cardiovascular disease. Chronotherapy and targeted sleep hygiene interventions offer promising adjunctive strategies for mitigating circadian misalignment in ADPKD. Timed administration of antihypertensives, diuretics, and disease-modifying agents, such as tolvaptan, along with melatonin supplementation, structured light exposure, and optimized physical activity patterns, may enhance therapeutic efficacy and improve quality of life (QoL). Future research should prioritize longitudinal and interventional studies incorporating circadian biomarkers to evaluate the impact of aligning therapeutic interventions with biological rhythms on kidney and cardiovascular outcomes in ADPKD.

papers.title: Association of annual household income and insomnia symptoms based on work-life balance among Japanese female workers in older adult care services: A cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Socioeconomic status has been associated with sleep disturbance; however, the link between annual household income and insomnia symptoms, considering the additive association with work-life balance, has yet to be examined. Therefore, we investigated this association among Japanese female care workers. Between 2015 and 2016, 451 women aged 18-60 years who worked in older adult care services were enrolled in this cross-sectional study. Insomnia symptoms were measured using the Athens Insomnia Scale. Categorized annual household income was divided into two categories (high/middle vs. low) based on the median annual household income from the national survey. Work-life balance was assessed by examining work-to-family and family-to-work conflicts. Exposure was defined as a combined category of income and work-life balance. Data were collected via self-administered questionnaires. Prevalence ratios (PRs) of insomnia symptoms were estimated using modified Poisson regression. The multivariable-adjusted PR (95% confidence interval [CI]) of insomnia symptoms was 1.43 (1.01-2.01) in the low- compared with the high/middle-income group.
