Compared with the group with high/middle income and better work-life balance, the PR (95% CI) of insomnia symptoms was 1.27 (0.80-2.00) among those with low income and better work-life balance. Meanwhile, high PRs were observed for both income groups with a worse work-life balance (2.00 [1.45-2.74] for high/middle income and 3.02 [2.00-4.56] for low income). Improving work-life balance may help mitigate insomnia symptoms regardless of income, while low income was associated with a higher prevalence of insomnia symptoms.

papers.title: The functional burden of chronic urticaria: Sleep quality, activity impairment and work productivity.
papers.abstract: Chronic urticaria (CU) is associated with a substantial disease burden extending beyond cutaneous manifestations. It may impair psychological well-being, sleep quality, daily functioning, and work productivity, although these domains have rarely been evaluated simultaneously. To investigate sleep quality, psychological status, activity impairment, and work productivity in patients with chronic urticaria and identify factors independently associated with the disease. This cross-sectional case-control study included 108 patients with chronic urticaria and 95 healthy controls. Sleep quality, psychological status, and work productivity were assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), Depression Anxiety Stress Scale-21 (DASS-21), and Work Productivity and Activity Impairment Questionnaire (WPAI). Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors independently associated with chronic urticaria. Patients with chronic urticaria had significantly poorer sleep quality, higher depression and anxiety scores, and greater activity impairment than controls (all p < 0.05). In multivariable analysis, higher PSQI, depression, stress, and activity impairment scores were independently associated with chronic urticaria (all p < 0.05). Among employed participants, absenteeism, presenteeism, and overall work productivity impairment were significantly greater in patients (all p < 0.001). Chronic urticaria is associated with impaired sleep quality, psychological distress, activity impairment, and reduced work productivity. These findings highlight the multidimensional burden of the disease and support a holistic, patient-centred approach to its management.

papers.title: Physical activity, sedentary behavior, sleep quality and the biological aging clocks.
papers.abstract: Physical activity (PA), sedentary behavior, and sleep quality are known lifestyle factors modulating the rate of aging but less is known about their putative interactions. We investigated the cross-sectional independent and interactive associations of these lifestyle factors with various biological aging clocks in adults of large age range. Eight hundred and ninety adults recruited from the INSPIRE-t cohort, aged 20 to 102 years old with a measure of at least one biological clock among PhenoAge, GrimAge, DunedinPACE, iAge, and intrinsic capacity (IC) clock, were included in the present study. PA levels, sitting time, and sleep deterioration were estimated using questionnaires. The associations of age acceleration/aging rate with each lifestyle factor and their interactions were explored through robust regressions adjusted for age, sex, education, and comorbidities. Main-term analyses showed that higher levels of PA were associated with reduced age acceleration for IC in women. Interaction analyses indicated that, in older adults, the adverse association of sleep deterioration with age acceleration/rate was attenuated with higher levels of PA for GrimAge, iAge, DunedinPACE, and IC clock or with a balanced combination of PA and sitting time for DunedinPACE and GrimAge. In the total population and in men, the detrimental association between sitting time and GrimAge was attenuated, or even reversed, with higher levels of PA, especially in individuals with good sleep quality. Our findings encourage increasing PA levels and limiting sedentary behavior or having an optimal combination of both in addition to maximizing sleep quality for preventing biological aging.
authors: I. H. U. HealthAge INSPIRE/Open Science study group

papers.title: A novel age-based physiological definition of adherence to pediatric long-term non-invasive ventilation: an exploratory study.
papers.abstract: The indications for pediatric long-term non-invasive ventilation (LT-NIV) have expanded. However, a standardized definition of pediatric adherence is lacking. To propose a novel physiological definition of adherence to pediatric LT-NIV and compare it with the two commonly used adult-derived definitions. Retrospective cross-sectional study including all eligible children aged 0.15-18 years enrolled in the LT-NIV follow-up program at Hospital Garrahan, Argentina. Clinical data were obtained from medical records and adherence from device memory downloads. The proposed definition classified patients as "adherent" when LT-NIV use reached ≥ 70% of the minimum age-specific recommended sleep duration (American Academy of Sleep Medicine consensus) on ≥ 70% of nights, replacing a fixed threshold with one tailored to each child´s sleep needs. This was compared to the current(≥ 4 h/night on ≥ 70% of nights) and classic (≥ 4 h/night on ≥ 50% of nights) adult-derived definitions. Eighty patients were included (median age 9.01years, IQR 5.96-14.09). The most frequent diagnoses were neuromuscular (31%) and genetic disorders (15%). LT-NIV was initiated electively in 91%, 75% reported sleep-disordered breathing symptoms, polysomnography was abnormal in 95.2%. Adherence rates were 66.25% (novel definition); 83.75% (classic definition) and 78.75% (current definition), p = 0.0005 and p = 0.0039 respectively. Poorer adherence was associated with younger age, developmental delay, absence of symptoms, earlier ventilation initiation and lower pressure settings. Our results highlight an overestimation of adherence when adult definitions are used. This first study explores a novel pediatric adherence definition for LT-NIV. Our research calls for action to discuss new international pediatric adherence thresholds.

papers.title: Italian adaptation of international recommendations for the management of restless legs syndrome: A consensus statement by the scientific committee of RLS-Italia.
papers.abstract: Recent international recommendations have substantially changed the management of restless legs syndrome (RLS), emphasizing systematic iron assessment, earlier use of iron therapy and α2δ ligands, and greater caution with chronic dopaminergic treatment because of augmentation. Their implementation requires adaptation to national healthcare organization, regulatory indications, reimbursement, and access to specialist services. The Scientific Committee of RLS-Italia conducted a structured, non-Delphi consensus process based on the 2025 American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline and systematic review, the 2026 RLS Foundation algorithm, the World Sleep Society partial endorsement, and selected supporting evidence. Successive drafts were circulated, discussed, and approved by all authors. The proposed Italian framework prioritizes clinical diagnosis, exclusion of mimics, correction of exacerbating factors, systematic assessment of iron status, and iron treatment when indicated. α2δ ligands are preferred for most adults with chronic persistent RLS, whereas dopamine agonists should be restricted to selected patients and monitored for augmentation. Refractory or augmented disease should be managed by clinicians with specific RLS expertise, with consideration of intravenous iron, opioids, or device-based treatment. Dipyridamole is not included in the standard pathway, and periodic limb movement disorder should not be diagnosed or treated solely on the basis of polysomnographic findings. This consensus statement provides a nationally coherent framework that can support regional implementation through locally appropriate organizational and clinical protocols.
papers.journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology

papers.title: Comment on: "The clinical relevance of sleep disturbance ('insomnia') in patients with advanced cancer receiving palliative care: a scoping review".
papers.journal: Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer

papers.title: Sleep Quality in Adults with Cancer: Associations with Symptom Burden and Psychological Resilience.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbance is prevalent among adults with cancer and often co-occurs with multiple physical and psychological symptoms. Although resilience has been associated with better sleep outcomes, evidence integrating overall symptom burden and resilience remains limited. To identify factors associated with sleep quality in adults with cancer, focusing on co-occurring symptom burden and resilience. This cross-sectional study included 159 adults with cancer recruited from a tertiary hospital and online patient communities in the Republic of Korea. Sleep quality was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. Symptom burden was measured with the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System 29-Item Profile, and resilience with the Korean version of the Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with poor sleep quality, and hierarchical multiple linear regression examined factors associated with sleep quality scores. The mean sleep quality score was 6.99 ± 3.84, and 42.1% of participants were classified as poor sleepers. Being 1-3 years postdiagnosis and having received radiotherapy were independently associated with higher odds of poor sleep. Higher mental health summary scores and higher resilience were associated with lower odds of poor sleep after adjustment for sociodemographic and clinical factors. The final regression model explained 34.1% of the variance in sleep quality. Poor sleep was common among adults with cancer. Mental health and resilience were independently associated with sleep quality beyond clinical characteristics. These findings highlight the relevance of considering psychosocial factors alongside clinical characteristics when assessing sleep problems in supportive oncology care.
papers.journal: Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer

papers.title: Slow-wave sleep selectively amplifies network signatures of the presumed epileptogenic zone in focal epilepsy.
papers.abstract: Slow-wave sleep increases interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs) and seizures in focal epilepsy, but how sleep stages reshape epileptogenic tissue remains unclear. We assessed whether sleep stages selectively modulate network properties of the presumed epileptogenic zone (pEZ) relative to irritative (IZ) and non-involved (NIZ) zones. We studied 22 patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy undergoing pre-surgical intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG). IED-free resting-state epochs spanned four vigilance stages: wakefulness, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep stages 2 and 3, and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Spectral power, functional connectivity, graph-theoretic indices, and the 1/f exponent were quantified across seven frequency bands. Sleep stage and zone interactions were tested using permutation testing. pEZ electrodes were classified using elastic net logistic regression with leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. NREM3 selectively amplified within-pEZ gamma-band synchrony beyond surrounding zones (pEZ-NIZ: d=1.204, P=0.027). pEZ local efficiency and betweenness centrality rose in beta1 and gamma bands versus wakefulness. The aperiodic exponent steepened within the IZ versus NIZ during NREM3 and NREM2 (d =1.452 and 0.87, P < 0.001 and P=0.015). A three-feature classifier (NREM3 aperiodic exponent, beta2 connectivity, gamma local efficiency) localised the pEZ without ictal recordings (median AUC 0.859 pEZ vs. non-pEZ). Slow-wave sleep selectively unmasks pEZ network properties via amplified power, synchrony and hub topology. NREM3-derived multimodal features may complement conventional pre-surgical biomarkers. Prospective validation in larger cohorts is needed to determine whether these markers improve surgical planning and outcome prediction.

papers.title: Pressure Injury Prevention in Advanced Cancer: A Narrative Review and Proposed Comfort-Prioritized, Risk-Stratified Framework.
papers.abstract: Patients with advanced cancer are particularly vulnerable to pressure injury (PI) because of immobility, symptom-related positioning constraints, moisture exposure, nutritional compromise, and progressive physiological deterioration. PIs can increase symptom burden and nursing complexity and substantially impair quality of life. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on PI risk assessment tools, risk factors, and preventive strategies for adults with advanced cancer. Evidence was drawn from oncology-specific validation and observational studies, palliative care literature, international clinical guidelines, and studies involving broader high-risk populations, with the directness and certainty of evidence distinguished for major recommendations. Oncology-specific evidence supports selected risk factors and assessment approaches, whereas much of the evidence for preventive interventions is extrapolated from non-oncology populations. Pressure-redistribution support surfaces, individualized repositioning, selective preventive dressings, nutritional care, and symptom management should therefore be tailored to PI risk, intervention burden, prognosis, patient preferences, and goals of care. To integrate these considerations, we propose a comfort-prioritized, risk-stratified conceptual framework for advanced cancer care. The framework supports individualized decision-making across palliative and actively dying phases while emphasizing both PI-related and patient-centered outcomes, including comfort, pain, sleep disruption, and goal-concordant care.

papers.title: Arthroscopic Matrix Augmentation of Partial-Thickness Rotator Cuff Tear Repairs Using a Full-Thickness Human Perinatal Tissue Allograft.
papers.abstract: Partial-thickness rotator cuff tears (PTRCTs) are common and many progress to full-thickness tears. A persistently symptomatic PTRCT can result in pain, weakness, sleep disturbances, and functional loss. The high incidence, reported progression rates, limited intrinsic healing capability, and functional impairments motivate investigation into effective surgical strategies when conservative care fails. Human perinatal tissue allografts have been previously used for full-thickness rotator cuff tear repair in limited instances, however their fragility makes arthroscopic handling challenging. Herein, we describe two patients who were successfully treated with perinatal tissue membrane allograft matrix augmentation (PTAMA) using an arthroscopic onlay technique after failed conservative care. The perinatal tissue allograft (MLG-COMPLETE; Samaritan Biologics) was found to have handling characteristics that could withstand arthroscopic manipulation and suturing. Following PTAMA, both patients had a significant reduction in pain levels (VAS) at 3 months and improved function (ASES and SANE) at final follow-up (13-15 months). No complications were seen in either patient. At final follow-up, strength and range of motion had returned to normal in both patients. PTRCTs are common and can be challenging to treat. Incorporation of an arthroscopic perinatal tissue membrane allograft onlay is feasible in symptomatic PTRCT after failed conservative treatments.

papers.title: Comparative assessment of AD8232- and MAX30003-based ECG acquisition paths using synthetic ECG signals.
papers.abstract: This study presents a comparative technical evaluation of two implemented electrocardiogram (ECG) acquisition paths based on AD8232 and MAX30003 under controlled laboratory conditions. The analog front-end paths were designed in accordance with the reference circuits and design recommendations specified in the manufacturer's documentation for the AD8232 and MAX30003 devices. Synthetic ECG signals were generated using a patient simulator for heart rates of 30, 60, 80, and 100 beats per minute and were recorded simultaneously from both acquisition paths at a sampling frequency of 128 Hz. The processing pipeline comprised time-axis standardization, baseline correction, local cross-correlation-based synchronization, linear amplitude alignment, QRS detection using a simplified Pan-Tompkins-inspired procedure, and median-centered amplitude standardization. Signal similarity after preprocessing was assessed using time-domain metrics, including Pearson correlation, mean absolute error, root mean square error (RMSE), and normalized RMSE. In addition, spectral analysis based on Welch's method was performed using absolute bandpower values and relative bandpower indices. After synchronization and normalization, both acquisition paths showed very high morphological agreement, with Pearson correlation exceeding 0.99 across all tested heart-rate settings. Error metrics remained low and comparable between recordings. Spectral analysis revealed marked differences in absolute power, reflecting properties of the complete acquisition chains rather than signal quality alone. Relative spectral indices showed implementation-specific differences between the complete acquisition paths, particularly in the 50 Hz component band, whereas the 40-60 Hz band was retained only as an auxiliary descriptive upper-band index because of the different filtering and digitization architectures of the two paths. Under the tested synthetic and controlled conditions, both implemented ECG acquisition paths provided comparable post-processed morphological representations of the ECG signal, while differing in spectral characteristics. The examined paths differed in the relative distribution of spectral energy under the applied configuration. However, these findings should be interpreted as implementation-specific technical observations rather than evidence of general device superiority. Further validation in human recordings and real-world conditions is required.

papers.title: Emerging evidence suggests that circadian disruption and muscle wasting form a self-reinforcing loop.
papers.abstract: Circadian disruption and skeletal muscle wasting frequently co-occur in critical illness, shift work, and aging. We propose a bidirectional self-reinforcing loop in which each process amplifies the other. Environmental disruption of the skeletal muscle clock impairs protein turnover and mitochondrial function, triggering atrophy. The resulting loss of muscle mass weakens peripheral clock output and disrupts systemic circadian rhythms. The forward arm is supported by genetic evidence, particularly from global Bmal1 knockout models and human sleep-deprivation studies. The reverse arm is supported by correlative evidence from clinical observations and disease models. Chronotherapeutic interventions targeting this loop have shown preclinical efficacy and warrant clinical translation.

papers.title: Relapsing Polychondritis With Severe Airway Involvement Mimicking Refractory Asthma: A Diagnostic Challenge.
papers.abstract: Relapsing polychondritis (RP) is a rare immune-mediated disorder that can cause severe tracheobronchial involvement and life-threatening airway compromise. We present a diagnostically challenging case of a 30-year-old non-binary patient whose progressive respiratory symptoms were initially attributed to severe refractory asthma. Despite repeated courses of systemic corticosteroids and escalation of asthma-directed therapy, they developed recurrent breathlessness, wheeze, and inspiratory stridor. Pulmonary function testing demonstrated severe fixed airflow obstruction with minimal bronchodilator reversibility and a flow-volume loop suggestive of central airway obstruction. Serial CT imaging subsequently demonstrated progressive smooth thickening and narrowing of the tracheobronchial tree, with relative sparing of the posterior membranous wall and no significant pulmonary parenchymal disease. These findings, together with the clinical course, exclusion of important alternative diagnoses, and multidisciplinary assessment by respiratory, rheumatology, radiology, and tertiary airway specialists, supported a clinicoradiological diagnosis of airway-dominant RP. Despite high-dose corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide followed by maintenance immunosuppression, the patient continued to experience severe airway compromise and recurrent respiratory symptoms. This case highlights the importance of considering RP in patients with treatment-refractory asthma-like symptoms, particularly when inspiratory stridor, fixed airflow obstruction, and progressive tracheobronchial abnormalities are present. Early recognition of central airway involvement and multidisciplinary assessment are essential to minimise irreversible airway damage.

papers.title: Numerical Examination of RIS-Enabled Microwave Imaging for Sleep Monitoring.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-enabled framework for microwave imaging aimed at non-invasive human monitoring in indoor environments. Our primary objective is to generate a representative reflectivity map of a resting or sleeping individual. This imaging can facilitate tracking of movements and biomarkers, such as breathing, during rest or sleep. Achieving this challenging task necessitates high signal strength, robustness against clutter, and minimal measurements to ensure fast data acquisition. To address these requirements, the proposed system utilizes programmable RIS configurations to manipulate the electromagnetic field distribution within the region of interest (ROI). In contrast to traditional methods, we combine radar-coincidence imaging (RCI) with computational imaging techniques. The former method yields high signal strength and facilitates clutter rejection, while the latter reduces the number of required measurements. Numerical simulations using a humanoid demonstrate the feasibility of reconstructing key features. The low number of measurements paves the way for fast image reconstruction and movement detection. Additionally, a comparative study with conventional random illumination is conducted, demonstrating improved reconstruction outcomes. These findings underscore the potential of RIS-enabled imaging for non-contact biomarker monitoring applications.
papers.journal: Proceedings. IEEE Antennas and Propagation Society. International Symposium

papers.title: Pharmacological inhibition of REV-ERBα ameliorates motor deficits in the 6-OHDA-lesioned mouse model of Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by nigrostriatal dopaminergic (DAergic) degeneration and motor dysfunction. Many PD patients also show circadian rhythm disturbances. Increasing evidence links circadian clock dysfunction to PD pathology. REV-ERBα is a circadian nuclear receptor that regulates DAergic genes under physiological conditions. However, its role in nigrostriatal dopamine (DA) homeostasis and motor function in PD remains unclear. In this study, we found elevated Rev-erbα mRNA expression in tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-positive neurons of the substantia nigra (SN) in a 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) mouse model of PD. To test its functional role, we assessed the acute effects of local SN microinjection of the REV-ERBα antagonist SR8278. We found that SR8278 partially recovered motor performance and improved fine motor function. These effects occurred regardless of circadian timing. SR8278 administration did not restore TH expression or tissue DA levels in the striatum and SN. However, in vivo microdialysis showed enhanced extracellular DA turnover in the striatum. Specifically, while extracellular DA metabolites level increased, basal extracellular DA levels showed no change. Together, these findings identify REV-ERBα as a potential therapeutic target that modulates extracellular nigrostriatal DA dynamics and improves motor function in PD.

papers.title: Biological age in the meta omics era: Integrating physical activity, sleep, and diet to reshape paths of healthy ageing.
papers.abstract: Biological age provides a translational endpoint linking modifiable lifestyle behaviors-physical activity, sleep, and diet-to multi-omics changes and downstream clinical outcomes. Integrating multiple ageing clocks with inflammatory, metabolic, and oxidative pathways supports reproducible, intervention-ready strategies to slow ageing and extend healthspan.

papers.title: Excessive Yawning During Escitalopram Therapy in a Rwandan Woman with Co-Morbid Depression and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Excessive yawning is an uncommon but recognized adverse effect of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). Although generally benign, it may cause distress and may be mistaken for a symptom of psychiatric or neurological illness. Case reports and pharmacovigilance data have linked escitalopram to yawning, sometimes in a dose-dependent manner. To our knowledge, this is one of the first reported cases of escitalopram-associated yawning in Rwanda. We describe a 44-year-old woman from rural Rwanda who presented with a severe depressive episode and comorbid post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Three days after starting escitalopram 10 mg daily, she reported markedly increased yawning, approximately six episodes every 15 minutes throughout the day, while her sleep and mood had begun to improve slightly. Medical and neurological causes, sleep-related causes and concurrent short-term diazepam use were considered and judged unlikely. The Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale score was 5, indicating a probable adverse drug reaction. Escitalopram was continued because of emerging antidepressant benefit, and the yawning had decreased substantially at the two-week follow-up. This case suggests that yawning occurring early in escitalopram treatment should be recognized as a probable adverse drug reaction. Awareness of this under-reported effect may prevent unnecessary investigations and premature discontinuation of an effective antidepressant.

papers.title: Pain and sleep disturbance were negatively associated with function and community mobility after hospitalization.
papers.abstract: The inconsistent nature of functional recovery after hospitalization points to gaps in our understanding of its determinants. The goal of this study was to examine associations between post-discharge pain interference and sleep disturbance on function and community mobility following hospitalization for medical illness. We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of data collected as part of a larger study evaluating a hospital-based mobility program. Participants were aged ≥60 and within one month of discharge from one of eight Veterans Affairs (VA) hospitals between September 2017 and August 2019. Data were collected through telephone surveys. Primary predictors of pain interference and sleep disturbance were measured by PROMIS-4 short forms. Outcomes were function measured by Late-Life Function and Disability Instruments (LLFDI overall function and advanced lower extremity function scores) and community mobility measured by Life Space. For each outcome, separate multiple linear regression models were fit including the key explanatory variables of interest and selected covariates. Participants (n = 618) were mean age 70.6 years, 95% male, 25% Black, and 34% lived alone; overall eight percent reported being discharged to a nursing home, and 15% being readmitted to the hospital. Overall, 39.9% of participants reported moderate/severe pain interference; of these, approximately half also reported at least some degree of sleep disturbance. Moderate/severe sleep disturbance was endorsed by 19%; of these, more than 75% also experienced some degree of pain interference. In adjusted models, pain interference and sleep disturbance were negatively associated with total function, lower extremity function, and community mobility (P-values <0.01). In this sample of recently hospitalized older adults, pain interference and sleep disturbance were independently associated with functional limitations and reduced community mobility. Primary care providers should consider assessing for pain and sleep problems during post-hospitalization visits to support optimal functional recovery.

papers.title: Sleep quality improvements and maintenance with exercise in older veterans with PTSD: Results from a pilot randomized trial.
papers.abstract: Identifying novel strategies to improve sleep quality among individuals with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is critically needed. The aim of the study was to evaluate the effects of exercise on sleep quality in older adults with PTSD participating in a 12-week pilot randomized trial of supervised exercise versus waitlist control. This study is a secondary analysis of a randomized, two-group design comparing multicomponent exercise to a waitlist control. Participants included 48 older Veterans with PTSD. The sample was, on average, 67.5 years old (SD = 3.6), primarily male (92%), and African American or Black (85%). At baseline, more than 90% of participants reported poor sleep quality. Linear models indicated medium effect size differences favoring the intervention group for PSQI global and daytime dysfunction (β's -0.31 to -0.40) and small effect size differences favoring the intervention group for PSQI sleep disturbance, sleep efficiency, sleep latency, sleep quality, and addendum for PTSD (βs -0.13 to -0.24). Within-group changes indicated small improvements in sleep quality in the exercise group (PSQI global, sleep disturbance, sleep duration, latency, quality; d's -0.11 to -0.26). In the control group, small deteriorations (PSQI global, sleep disturbance, daytime of dysfunction, use of sleep medications, sleep efficiency, sleep latency, PTSD sleep addendum) were found. There was no evidence of mediation in the exploratory mediation analysis evaluating the effect of PTSD symptom severity on the relationship between intervention condition (supervised exercise or control) and sleep quality. Findings provide preliminary evidence for exercise as a complementary intervention to maintain or improve sleep quality in this population.

papers.title: Deciphering interventional dynamical causality from non-intervention complex systems.
papers.abstract: Detecting and quantifying causal influence is a focal topic in the fields of science, engineering, and interdisciplinary studies. However, causal studies on non-intervention systems attract much attention but remain extremely challenging. The delay-embedding technique provides a promising approach. In this study, we propose a framework named interventional dynamical causality (IntDC) in contrast to the traditional constructive dynamical causality (ConDC). ConDC, including Granger causality, transfer entropy, and convergence of cross-mapping, measures the causality by constructing a dynamical model without considering interventions. A computational criterion, interventional embedding entropy (IEE), is proposed to measure causal strengths in an interventional manner. IEE is an intervened causal information flow but in the delay-embedding space. Further, the IEE theoretically and numerically enables the deciphering of IntDC solely from observational (non-interventional) time-series data, without requiring any knowledge of dynamical models or real interventions in the considered system. In particular, IEE can be applied to rank causal effects according to their importance and construct causal networks from data. We conducted numerical experiments on logistic dynamics, coupled-Hénon maps, and chaotic neural networks to demonstrate that IEE can find causal edges accurately, eliminate effects of confounding, and quantify causal strength robustly over traditional indices. We also applied IEE to real-world tasks, including estimating neural connectomes of Caenorhabditis elegans, detecting COVID-19 transmission networks in Japan, and investigating regulatory networks surrounding key circadian genes. IEE performed as an accurate and robust tool for causal analyses solely from the observational data. Both the IntDC framework and the IEE algorithm proposed in this study provide an approach to understanding causal influence in diverse non-intervention complex systems.

papers.title: Associations of Mechanistically Partitioned Type 2 Diabetes Polygenic Risk With Psychiatric and Related Phenotypes in UK Biobank.
papers.abstract: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) and psychiatric disorders frequently co-occur; however, it remains unclear whether this overlap is generalized or defined by particular T2D mechanisms and psychiatric phenotypes. We investigated whether genetically defined T2D pathways show distinct associations with psychiatric and related phenotypes. We calculated polygenic risk scores (PRSs) for 8 mechanistic T2D clusters and tested associations with psychiatric and sleep phenotypes and chronic pain in the UK Biobank. The study included 408,063 White British participants (54.1% female) and 50,214 non-overlapping White European participants (56.2% female). Models incorporated demographic, socioeconomic, lifestyle, anthropometric, and medication factors, with false discovery rate (FDR) correction across all tests. Adiposity PRS showed the broadest associations. Body-fat distribution PRS was associated with atypical major depressive disorder across all models, whereas obesity-mediated insulin-resistance PRS was associated only in the minimally adjusted model. Neither PRS was associated with nonatypical depression after FDR correction. Body-fat PRS was associated with generalized anxiety disorder, mood instability, long sleep duration, and chronic pain in all models. Associations for the other pathways were more selective and were concentrated in sleep duration and chronotype; metabolic-syndrome PRS was consistently associated with neuroticism. Cross-sample support was strongest for the association between obesity-mediated insulin-resistance PRS and morning chronotype. The overlap between T2D and psychiatric phenotypes was heterogeneous, with the strongest evidence for adiposity PRS and atypical depression and with more selective associations across other pathways. Considering heterogeneity in both T2D biology and psychiatric presentation may help clarify shared mechanisms.

papers.title: Latent profile analysis of adolescent quality of life and its associations with lifestyle behaviors.
papers.abstract: Adolescent quality of life (QoL) is critical for development, yet its heterogeneity is underexplored. We aimed to identify latent QoL profiles and examine associations with lifestyle behaviors. Latent profile analysis (LPA) was performed on 7,244 Chinese adolescents (49.3% boys) using the Quality of Life Scale for Children and Adolescents. Multinomial logistic regression tested links between QoL profiles and sleep duration, physical activity, screen time, ultra-processed foods (UPF), and minimally processed foods (MPF), adjusting for demographics. Five profiles emerged: Low QoL (C1), Health-advantaged (C2), Moderate QoL (C3), Low Physical and Psychological Health (C4), and High QoL (C5). Relative to C3, longer sleep duration was associated with lower odds of C1 (OR = 0.83) and C2 (OR = 0.74), but higher odds of C4 (OR = 1.26) and C5 (OR = 1.27). Higher physical activity was associated with lower odds of C2 (OR = 0.71) and higher odds of C4 (OR = 1.41) and C5 (OR = 1.62). Screen time was associated with lower odds of C2 and higher odds of C4. Greater MPF intake was associated with lower odds of C1 (OR = 0.70) and C2 (OR = 0.61), and higher odds of C4 (OR = 1.78) and C5 (OR = 1.35). Higher UPF intake was associated with lower odds of C1 (OR = 0.25), C2 (OR = 0.54), and C5 (OR = 0.56), and higher odds of C4 (OR = 1.45). Relative to the Moderate QoL class, lifestyle behaviors showed distinct associations with QoL profiles. Sleep duration, physical activity, and MPF intake were associated with lower odds of the Health-advantaged class and higher odds of the Low Physical and Psychological Health and High QoL classes. UPF intake was inversely associated with Low QoL, Health-advantaged, and High QoL classes, and positively associated with the Low Physical and Psychological Health class. These findings highlight the heterogeneity of adolescent QoL and suggest that interventions should be tailored to specific QoL profiles.

papers.title: Impact of an Informational Video on Parental Choice of Tonsillectomy Technique.
papers.abstract: To evaluate whether the use of an educational video explaining the differences between intracapsular and extracapsular tonsillectomy, as well as their respective risks and benefits, influences parental decision-making in a pediatric otolaryngology clinic. Flyers with a quick response (QR) code linking to a video that explained intracapsular versus extracapsular tonsillectomy techniques and associated complications were posted in exam rooms of a pediatric otolaryngology clinic in July 2024. Parents were encouraged to view the video. Data were collected for tonsillectomies performed between May 2024 and January 2025, including clinic visit date, patient age and gender, parent at the visit, indication for tonsillectomy, and procedure chosen. Of 214 patients, 133 (62%) had clinic visits before flyers were posted and 81 (38%) after. Before the flyers, only 24 (18%) chose intracapsular tonsillectomy, compared to 34 (42%) afterward (P < .001). Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) or sleep disordered breathing (SDB) were the most common surgical indications (N = 200, 94%). Patient age and gender, parent at visit, and surgical indication were not significantly associated with the procedure chosen. These findings suggest educational interventions can influence parental preference for tonsillectomy type. Providing accessible, comprehensible information may support more informed decision-making, potentially improving surgical outcomes and parent satisfaction. Integrating concise educational tools into clinic visits offers a practical way to enhance communication and engage families in shared surgical decision-making. These interventions may also standardize information delivery and reduce variability in how options are presented across providers.

papers.title: Short-term responses across two sequential plant-based activity sessions: an exploratory fixed-order pilot study.
papers.abstract: Structured plant-based activities combine natural materials, purposeful manual work, sensory engagement, and social interaction, but direct comparisons of practical formats in community adults remain limited. We characterized short-term responses during two sequential sessions and compared within-session changes. Twenty-five adults participated in a single-group, fixed-order pilot study. Session 1 involved horticultural crafting; 1 week later, Session 2 involved balm crafting followed by horticultural crafting. Twenty-three attended both sessions. DASS-21 and STAI-S were principal outcomes; horticultural wellbeing, HRV, and forehead single-channel EEG were exploratory. Within-session changes and complete-case between-session differences were estimated with 95% CIs. Post hoc TOST examined exploratory equivalence bounds. Both sessions were followed by favorable short-term psychological changes. DASS-21 scores decreased by 8.57 points in Session 1 [95% CI (5.41, 11.72), n = 23] and 5.53 in Session 2 [(2.65, 8.41), n = 17]. STAI-S scores decreased by 7.30 points in Session 1 [(5.23, 9.37), n = 25] and 6.86 in Session 2 [(4.07, 9.66), n = 22]; all four Holm-adjusted p values were <0.001. Complete-case comparisons showed no statistically detectable between-session difference in DASS-21 improvement [3.12 points, 95% CI (-1.51, 7.75)] or STAI-S improvement [0.34 points, (-3.15, 3.83)]. STAI-S changes met the exploratory TOST criterion only at the broad ±0.50 standardized bound. Horticultural wellbeing improved in both sessions; SDNN and RMSSD increased, whereas EEG findings did not remain significant after multiplicity correction. Both sessions were associated with favorable short-term psychological changes, particularly reduced distress and state anxiety. These findings support the feasibility and potential value of brief, hands-on plant-based activities in community settings and provide estimates for larger randomized, counterbalanced trials. Given the fixed order and absence of a control group, the findings are preliminary rather than definitive causal or modality-specific evidence.

papers.title: Electroencephalography Changes in Emotional Recognition: A Signal Processing Approach Using Wavelet Features.
papers.abstract: motion recognition using electroencephalography (EEG) has gained significant attention in the fields of affective computing and human-computer interaction due to its ability to capture real-time neural responses. EEG signal variations associated with emotional states can be analysed using wavelet-based signal processing within the arousal-valence framework. This study aims to analyse EEG signal variations associated with emotional states using a wavelet-based signal processing approach within the arousal-valence framework. A prospective observational study was conducted on 48 healthy participants. Emotional states were induced using image, video and music stimuli categorised under the arousal-valence model. EEG signals were recorded using the standard 10-20 electrode placement system. The acquired signals were pre-processed and analysed using discrete wavelet transform (DWT) to extract time-frequency features, including energy and entropy. Statistical analysis was performed to evaluate hemispheric differences and gender-based variations. Differences in EEG activity were observed between the left and right hemispheres across multiple emotional states (p < .05). Video and music stimuli produced stronger and more distinguishable EEG responses compared to image-based stimuli. Negative emotions demonstrated higher discriminative patterns than positive emotions. Gender-based variations were also observed in EEG responses. Wavelet-based EEG feature analysis provides meaningful and discriminative information for emotion recognition and may provide a robust feature set for future machine learning-based emotion recognition systems. Further studies incorporating classification algorithms and larger data sets are required to validate their predictive performance.

papers.title: How short-video usage influences college students' daily lives: empirical evidence from sleep, self-perception, daily life conditions, and emotional state.
papers.abstract: As the popularity of short-video apps rises among university students, issues have been identified linking problematic engagement to sleep, self-control, cognitive abilities, and emotion. However, the effects of bedtime procrastination and executive dysfunction on this relationship remain unknown. A cross-sectional study was conducted among 538 Chinese university students using an anonymous online survey. Pearson correlation analyses, observed variable path analysis, and indirect effect analyses were performed using the structural equation modeling framework. Short-video addiction, bedtime procrastination, executive dysfunction, and emotional disturbance were found to be positively correlated. Within the structural model, executive dysfunction was found to correlate positively and significantly with emotional disturbance (β = 0.679, p < 0.001), whereas short-video addiction was found to be less strongly correlated (β = 0.133, p = 0.001). Furthermore, the correlation between bedtime procrastination and emotional disturbance was reduced to insignificance when executive dysfunction was added to the model (β = 0.018, p > 0.05). Model fit was inconsistent, showing adequate incremental fit but inadequate RMSEA fit. It seems that executive dysfunctions play a significant role in emotional distress in problematic short-video users compared to bedtime procrastination. As this research was cross-sectional and self-report-based, causation cannot be established. Interventions should concentrate on the enhancement of executive functions and self-regulation abilities rather than screen time reduction only.

papers.title: An explainable machine learning model based on multidimensional task-state electroencephalography for identifying attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder comorbid developmental dyslexia.
papers.abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and developmental dyslexia (DD) are highly comorbid, yet objective differentiation from individual disorders remains challenging due to the lack of neurophysiological biomarkers. This study aimed to develop an interpretable machine learning model leveraging multidimensional task-state EEG features to distinguish ADHD-DD comorbidity from ADHD and typical development (TD). Ninety children (27 ADHD-DD, 40 ADHD, 23 TD) underwent EEG during a VSWM task. Five feature categories were extracted: event-related potentials, time-frequency characteristics, functional connectivity, graph-theoretic metrics, and nonlinear dynamics. Three feature-processing strategies and nine classifiers were compared within a nested cross-validation framework. Feature contribution was quantified by coefficient back-projection of the optimal PCA-LR mode. Sensitivity and permutation analyses were performed. The PCA-LR model achieved a balanced accuracy of 80.5%, a Macro-F1 of 0.799, and a Macro-AUC of 0.912. Class-wise AUCs were 0.905 for ADHD-DD, 0.904 for ADHD, and 0.927 for TD. Left temporal α-band functional connectivity was a shared high-contribution feature in both disorder groups. ADHD-DD was distinguished by widely distributed cross-regional connectivity spanning θ and α bands and by P200 amplitude. ADHD was characterized primarily by α-band network metrics and α-ERD, whereas TD relied mainly on θ and α bands functional connectivity and graph-theoretic metrics. Our findings suggest that multidimensional task-state EEG features may help differentiate children with ADHD-DD comorbidity from those with ADHD or typical development. They also indicate that machine-learning approaches may be useful for identifying neurodevelopmental comorbid conditions.

papers.title: A sliding window and Fourier decomposition method based 1D-CNN framework for motor imagery EEG classification.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) signal classification is fundamental requirement for effective motor imagery (MI) brain-computer interface (BCI) applications. However, current MI classification methods often depend on handcrafted spatial filtering or complex time-frequency transformations that increase computational complexity. To mitigate this limitation, we propose a unified architecture that integrates a sliding window (SW), a Fourier decomposition method (FDM), and a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) for MI-EEG classification. The raw EEG data were segmented using the SW approach to augment the data and extract more temporal feature patterns from each trial. The segmented signal, containing time-domain features, was subsequently processed using a band-pass filter and FDM to extract frequency-based features. Here, FDM decomposes the signal into eight orthogonal Fourier Intrinsic Band Functions (FIBFs). A 1D-CNN architecture was employed to learn representations from the decomposed EEG signals. The proposed framework was evaluated on the BCI Competition III Dataset IVa (BCIC III IVa) and BCI Competition IV-2a (BCIC IV 2a) datasets. Our method achieved accuracies of 79.14% and 93.67% on the BCIC IV 2a and BCIC III IVa datasets, respectively, under the subject-dependent evaluation protocol. To evaluate cross-subject generalization, the proposed framework was validated using the Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) protocol, achieving average classification accuracies of 76.49% on the BCIC III Dataset IVa and 55.50% on the BCIC IV 2a dataset. Furthermore, deployment on the NVIDIA Jetson Nano demonstrated complete pipeline latencies of 58.119 ms/trial and 85.055 ms/trial, corresponding to throughputs of 17.21 and 11.76 trials/s for the BCIC III IVa and BCIC IV 2a datasets, respectively. The results show the strong potential of the developed MI-EEG classification method to assist subjects with motor ailments.

papers.title: Effects of multiple low-dose intranasal dexmedetomidine administration on postoperative pulmonary complications in elderly patients undergoing thoracoscopic radical resection of lung cancer: a single-center randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) ranging from 30% to 50% have been recognized as a major threat to postoperative recovery. Current conventional interventions cannot effectively reduce the occurrence of PPCs. In this study, we aimed to investigate the effects of multiple low-dose intranasal dexmedetomidine administration on PPCs in elderly patients. In this double-blind, randomized, controlled trial, elderly patients were randomly assigned at a 1:1 ratio to receive multiple low-dose intranasal dexmedetomidine administration (MD group) or normal saline nasal spray (NS group). The primary outcome was the incidence of PPCs within 7 days after surgery. Key secondary outcomes included the severity grading and classification of PPCs. Other secondary outcomes included serum interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) levels, Richards-Campbell sleep questionnaire (RCSQ) scores at predefined time points, and adverse reactions. A total of 190 patients were screened, and 186 completed the study. The incidence of PPCs was significantly lower in the MD group than in the NS group (9.68% vs. 22.58%, P = 0.017), with a risk ratio (RR) of 2.333 [95% confidence interval (CI): 1.173-6.317], absolute risk reduction (ARR) of 12.90%, and number needed to treat (NNT) of 7.75. Sensitivity analyses using the per-protocol population (PP) dataset yielded consistent results, confirming the stability and reliability of the primary outcome. The distribution of severity grading of PPCs also differed significantly between the groups (P = 0.036). After Bonferroni correction, the between-group difference in PPCs severity grading was not statistically significant (corrected P = 0.072). The distribution of pneumonia also differed significantly between the groups (P = 0.029). There were significant group effects, time effects, and interaction effects for IL-6, TNF-α, and RCSQ in the two groups after surgery (all P < 0.05). No significant between-group differences were observed in drug-related adverse events. Multiple low-dose intranasal dexmedetomidine administration significantly reduces the incidence of PPCs in elderly patients undergoing radical thoracoscopic lung-cancer resection with a favorable safety profile. https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=243165; identifier ChiCTR2400090593.

papers.title: Tensor decomposition reveals discrete cortical reorganization under graded propofol anesthesia.
papers.abstract: Although propofol-induced anesthesia is known to suppress consciousness by promoting low-frequency frontal oscillations through thalamocortical circuits, a comprehensive understanding of its whole-brain coupling feature set remains elusive. Specifically, the global reorganization of nonlinear cross-frequency coupling remains poorly characterized due to analytical limitations. We analyzed 64-channel EEG data from 17 participants across five states (awake and target propofol concentrations of 1, 2, 3, and 4 mcg/ml, defined as States 1 to 5). After computing time-frequency representation (TFR) and bicoherence, Parallel Factor Analysis (PARAFAC) was used to extract unbiased spatio-spectral components from both linear and nonlinear measures. PARAFAC decomposition isolated distinct linear and nonlinear neurodynamic components driving the anesthetic transition. While linear spectral features and signal complexity transitioned in a gradual, monotonic manner. PARAFAC tensor decomposition of high-dimensional whole-brain bicoherence identified two robust, intrinsically decoupled nonlinear components with distinct spatial-spectral profiles. Model comparison demonstrated that frontal slow-wave self-coupling (Component 1) undergoes a discrete, stepwise state-space reconfiguration during loss of consciousness, whereas posterior alpha coupling (Component 2) exhibits a smooth, continuous decay with propofol titration. Phase-space kinetic trajectories confirmed a highly directed transition at unconsciousness onset, followed by confined local oscillations during deep anesthesia. This multi-dimensional decomposition framework captures discrete versus continuous neural dynamics, providing objective, state-sensitive biomarkers for precisely monitoring anesthesia depth and cortical state transitions.

papers.title: A comparative evaluation of thiol/disulfide homeostasis and ischemia-modified albumin levels in patients with heroin use disorder in remission and detoxification.
papers.abstract: Chronic heroin use disturbs body's redox (oxidant-antioxidant) balance, together with dynamic thiol-disulfide balance and ischemia-modified albumin; which are two distinct blood markers that may reflect the oxidative and ischemic load in substance dependence. It is still unclear whether these markers change across the clinical phases of heroin use disorder (HUD), or whether they relate to the affective and behavioral symptoms that dominate the clinical picture. In this cross-sectional study, 101 adults meeting DSM-5 criteria for HUD were split into a remission group (n = 52) and a detoxification group (n = 49). We measured serum native and total thiol, disulfide, the disulfide/native thiol, disulfide/total thiol and native thiol/total thiol ratios, and IMA. Participants also completed a symptom inventory, a craving measure, and scales for healthy-lifestyle behavior and nutrition attitude. Groups were compared with Student's t-test or the Mann-Whitney U test, categorical variables with chi-square or Fisher's exact test; associations were tested with Spearman correlations, and predictors of total thiol and IMA with multiple linear regression. Patients in detoxification group scored markedly higher on depression, anxiety, anger, somatic symptoms, suicidal ideation, psychosis, sleep disturbance, dissociation and craving (all p ≤ 0.001), and lower on healthy-lifestyle and nutrition-attitude scores (p < 0.001). In contrast, no thiol/disulfide measure or IMA differed between phases. IMA correlated positively with depression (r = 0.254) and craving (r = 0.209); whereas the disulfide/thiol ratios correlated negatively, and native thiol/total thiol positively with healthy-lifestyle and nutrition-attitude scores. Regression models for total thiol and IMA were not statistically significant. In HUD, redox and ischemia markers appear to follow symptom severity; especially depression, craving and health behavior, rather than the treatment phase itself. IMA, in particular, may reflect an oxidative and inflammatory component of mood regulation and craving.

papers.title: Acupuncture combined with transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation for chronic postpartum insomnia comorbid with emotional disorders: a case report.
papers.abstract: Postpartum women constitute a vulnerable population in whom insomnia comorbid with emotional disorders such as anxiety and depression is disproportionately prevalent, attributable to hormonal fluctuations, environmental changes, and social role transitions. This comorbidity significantly increases their long-term risk of mental health disorders. Given the safety concerns of sedative-hypnotic medications, non-pharmacological therapies are the first-line treatment for this population. We report the case of a 34-year-old woman with chronic postpartum insomnia comorbid with emotional disorders, who provided written informed consent for the publication of her de-identified clinical data and received 4 weeks of combined acupuncture and transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) treatment. Clinical assessments were performed at baseline, week 2, week 4 (end of treatment), and week 8 (4-week post-treatment follow-up) using validated scales including the PSQI, ISI, and HAMA, among others. After 4 weeks of treatment, the patient demonstrated significant improvements in objective sleep quality and anxiety symptoms, while subjective insomnia perception and depressive symptoms remained partially unresolved. Notably, all clinical outcomes continued to improve to near-normal levels during the follow-up period without any additional intervention, and no adverse events were recorded. This case demonstrates that combined acupuncture and taVNS is a safe and effective intervention for chronic postpartum insomnia comorbid with emotional disorders, with a favorable sustained therapeutic effect after treatment cessation, offering a valuable alternative for non-pharmacological management in this population.

papers.title: Bile acid metabolism and signaling in human and animal health: A One Health perspective.
papers.abstract: The One Health concept emphasizes the interdependence of human, animal, and ecosystem health. Against this broad backdrop, bile acids (BAs), as central products of host-microbiota co-metabolism, act far beyond their classical role in lipid emulsification. This review systematically summarizes BA biosynthesis, enterohepatic circulation, and gut microbiota-mediated metabolic modification. We highlight how gut microbiota-derived secondary BAs and farnesoid X receptor and Takeda G protein-coupled receptor 5-mediated BA signaling together shape BA homeostasis, glucose and lipid metabolism, intestinal barrier integrity, and immune homeostasis. We further discuss how population diversity, circadian rhythm, diet, behavior, environmental exposure, and surgical interventions dynamically shape systemic BA profiles. Finally, from a One Health perspective, we highlight the translational potential of BA-targeted strategies in hepatobiliary diseases, metabolic disorders, neurodegenerative and retinal degenerative diseases, and intestinal infections, as well as their value in animal production as non-antibiotic nutritional regulators. By improving animal health and reducing excessive drug use, residues, and risks of antimicrobial resistance at the source, BA-based precision nutrition may contribute to food safety and ecosystem health. Overall, this review positions BAs as key molecular hubs in One Health, linking host metabolism, gut microbiota, immune regulation, and the integrated health of humans, animals, and ecosystems.

papers.title: Beyond a Single Hypoxic Burden Value: Hypoxic Burden Ratio Assessed by Peripheral Arterial Tonometry in Obstructive Sleep Apnea.
papers.abstract: Hypoxic burden (HB) integrates the depth and duration of nocturnal oxygen desaturation in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), but a single HB value may conceal distinct hypoxemic profiles. We explored the relationship between two automated HB measures derived from peripheral arterial tonometry-based home sleep apnea testing (PAT-HSAT) data: desaturation area under the SpO2 baseline (HB_baseline) and area under 90% SpO2 (HB_<90%). We performed a retrospective cross-sectional study of 2136 adults with OSA, diagnosed by a peripheral arterial tonometry-derived apnea-hypopnea index based on 3% desaturation criteria (pAHI3%) ≥5 events/h. Three operational HB groups were designated according to the relationship between HB_baseline and HB_<90%. Type 1 was characterized by measurable HB_baseline (>0%·min/h) and HB_<90% = 0%·min/h; the HB_baseline/HB_<90% ratio was not calculable because the denominator was zero. Among patients with measurable HB_<90%, Type 2 was defined by an HB ratio ≥1 and Type 3 by an HB ratio <1. These three groups were prespecified as exploratory operational categories. Type 1, Type 2, and Type 3 comprised 506 (23.7%), 1108 (51.9%), and 522 (24.4%) patients, respectively. The percentage of total sleep time (TST) with SpO2 below 90% (T90) had median values of 0.1%, 5.4%, and 63.6% in Types 1, 2, and 3, respectively. Types 2 and 3 had similar median pAHI3% (26.3 and 28.8 events/h) but markedly different median HB_<90% (6.0 and 86.5%·min/h). HB_baseline correlated strongly with pAHI3% across all groups (Spearman ρ, 0.9295-0.9378), whereas HB_<90% correlated moderately with pAHI3% in Types 2 and 3 (ρ=0.6292 and 0.6209; all P<0.001). The relative magnitude of HB_baseline and HB_<90% provides an exploratory operational framework for describing distinct hypoxemic profiles in OSA beyond a single HB value. The framework is descriptive and hypothesis-generating; its clinical, prognostic, mechanistic, and therapeutic utility has not been established and requires external and longitudinal validation.

papers.title: Copenhagen Magnetic Personalized Accelerated Brain Circuit Therapy (CoMPACT) trial: study protocol for a randomized, double-blinded, sham-controlled, three-armed, parallel-group trial of transcranial magnetic stimulation for treatment-resistant depression.
papers.abstract: Treatment-resistant depression (TRD), characterized by poor response to conventional antidepressant therapies, remains a major clinical challenge. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) has emerged as a promising alternative. Employing intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS), TMS protocols have yielded rapid antidepressant effects in recent accelerated treatment studies. These findings warrant further investigation in larger samples to confirm efficacy and in-depth investigation into the underlying mechanisms. Moreover, other cortical sites may also represent suitable targets for accelerated iTBS treatment of TRD. This randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial will assess the efficacy, feasibility and mechanisms of a novel, personalized, and accelerated iTBS protocol for TRD, targeting two left hemispheric regions, the left dlPFC and inferior parietal lobule (IPL), both characterized by anticorrelated functional connectivity with the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex. 78 adults (aged 18-95 years) will be recruited from Danish mental health centers and randomly assigned to one of three groups: (1) active iTBS of the left dlPFC, (2) active iTBS targeting of the left IPL, or (3) sham iTBS at either site. The intervention includes five daily sessions over five consecutive days. Targeting informed by group-level functional connectivity will be combined with individualized coil placement and stimulation dosing using electric field modeling based on whole-brain anatomical magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Antidepressant efficacy will be evaluated using the 6-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale as the primary outcome, assessed at an early post-intervention follow-up (F1) within three days after the final stimulation session. Multimodal post-treatment assessments, including MRI, will be conducted within five days after the intervention (T1). A four-week follow-up (T2) will assess the durability of clinical and cognitive outcomes. Neurophysiological mechanisms will be investigated using electroencephalography as well as structural and functional MRI. By testing a novel stimulation protocol and evaluating the efficacy of a new parietal target, this study will help advance the development of innovative, circuit-based interventions for TRD, with potential implications for broader applications across neuropsychiatry. https://clinicaltrials.gov/, identifier NCT06895863.

papers.title: Current situation and influencing factors of oral frailty among community-dwelling older adults with chronic diseases in China: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: To examine the prevalence and associated factors of oral frailty among community-dwelling older adults with chronic diseases in minority communities in Northeast China. A cross-sectional study was conducted from November to December 2023 using convenience sampling in three communities in Yanji City, Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture. Participants aged 60 years and older with at least one diagnosed chronic disease and a minimum of four natural teeth completed the Mandarin Chinese versions of the Oral Frailty Index-8 (OFI-8), the FRAIL scale, the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and the Attitudes to Aging Questionnaire (AAQ). Binary logistic regression was used to identify factors independently associated with oral frailty. Among 393 valid participants, oral frailty was identified in 280 individuals, yielding a prevalence of 71.2% (OFI-8 score: 5.61 ± 2.58). The most frequently reported OFI-8 items were difficulty eating hard food (62.3%), choking (48.6%), and dry mouth (45.8%). After adjustment, advanced age, female sex, low personal monthly income, both low and high BMI, alcohol consumption, physical frailty, sleep disturbance, a negative attitude toward aging, having three or more chronic diseases, and diabetes mellitus were independently associated with oral frailty (all p < 0.05). Oral frailty is highly prevalent among older adults with chronic diseases in minority communities of Northeast China and is independently associated with multimorbidity, particularly diabetes. Screening for oral frailty should be integrated into routine community-based chronic disease management, with targeted prevention efforts focusing on modifiable behavioral and psychosocial determinants.

papers.title: Chronopharmacological effects of 5-aminosalicylic acid in the treatment of experimental colitis in mice.
papers.abstract: 5-Aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA) is a first-line therapy for ulcerative colitis, but whether dosing timing influences its therapeutic efficacy remains unclear. This study aims to investigate the chronopharmacological effects of 5-ASA in experimental colitis. A dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis model was used to compare the therapeutic effects of 5-ASA administered at different Zeitgeber times. Colonic proteomic profiling was performed to identify circadian-responsive proteins associated with differential drug efficacy. Intestinal epithelial-specific Bmal1 knockout mice were used to determine whether the circadian clock regulates the chronopharmacological response to 5-ASA. 5-ASA showed marked time-dependent efficacy in DSS-induced colitis, with greater protection at ZT14 than at ZT2. Proteomic analysis identified ferritin heavy chain 1 (FTH1) as a circadian-responsive protein associated with differential treatment outcomes. 5-ASA suppressed FTH1 expression, whereas FTH1 overexpression attenuated anti-inflammatory effects of 5-ASA. Moreover, intestinal epithelial-specific deletion of Bmal1 largely abolished diurnal variation in both FTH1 expression and 5-ASA efficacy, indicating that the intestinal clock coordinates the time-dependent response to 5-ASA. These findings identify FTH1 as a circadian-responsive factor linked to the time-dependent efficacy of 5-ASA and support circadian-guided optimization of 5-ASA administration as a potential strategy for improving UC treatment.

papers.title: Structural, dielectric behavior, diffuse phase transition, and electrical properties of 0.7(Bi1-x Sm x ) FeO3-0.3BaTiO3 ceramics (x = 0.1 and 0.2).
papers.abstract: Environmentally friendly 0.7(Bi1-x Sm x )FeO3-0.3BaTiO3 systems with various doping rates with x = 0.1 and 0.2, have been synthesized by the solid-state method, and their structural, microstructural, vibrational, and electrical properties were systematically investigated. X-ray diffraction combined with Rietveld refinement confirmed the stabilization of a single-phase perovskite structure, with lattice contraction attributed to Sm3+ substitution. The BFBT-0.1Sm composition crystallizes in a tetragonal phase with P4/mmm symmetry, whereas the BFBT-0.2Sm sample adopts an orthorhombic structure belonging to the Pmmm space group. This structural evolution is consistently supported by both XRD patterns and Raman spectral analysis. SEM analysis revealed dense microstructures with well-distributed grains. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) confirmed the presence of all the chemical elements constituting the materials. Raman spectroscopy provided evidence of local structural distortion. Dielectric measurements showed a significant increase in permittivity, while impedance and AC conductivity analyses indicated a thermally activated hopping mechanism consistent with Jonscher's power law. The dielectric constant varies with temperature, indicating the occurrence of a diffuse phase transition. This behavior was further analyzed using the modified Curie-Weiss law. A thorough analysis of the dielectric properties as a function of temperature demonstrates a characteristic ferroelectric to paraelectric (FE-PE) transition, marked by a significant rise in the real part of permittivity near 600-700 K for both compounds. This substantial permittivity underscores their potential for energy storage applications. These findings suggest that the studied ceramics are promising candidates for multifunctional devices.

papers.title: Sex-specific clinical profiles in patients with acute ischemic stroke and chronic kidney disease.
papers.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is common among patients with acute ischemic stroke (AIS) and is associated with worse outcomes. Although sex-related differences in stroke are well recognized, it remains unclear whether clinical characteristics associated with sex differ according to CKD status. We characterized sex-associated clinical profiles among patients with AIS with and without documented CKD. We conducted a retrospective analysis of the PRISMA Health Stroke Registry. Baseline characteristics were compared between patients with and without documented CKD in the overall cohort and after stratification by sex. Multivariable logistic regression with backward likelihood-ratio selection was used to identify independent clinical characteristics associated with documented CKD in the overall cohort and with male sex within the CKD and non-CKD subgroups. Adjusted odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. Internal stability was assessed using bootstrap resampling. Among 5,469 patients with AIS, 447 (8.2%) had documented CKD. Independent characteristics associated with CKD included prosthetic heart valve (OR, 3.73), elevated serum creatinine (OR, 2.79), obesity (OR, 2.51), heart failure (OR, 2.21), hypertension (OR, 2.20), African American race (OR, 2.11), and depression (OR, 1.97). In stratified analyses, associations of male sex with sleep apnea, smoking, and diastolic blood pressure ≥80 mmHg were numerically stronger in the CKD group than in the non-CKD group: sleep apnea, OR 4.62 vs. 2.38; smoking, OR 3.19 vs. 1.31; and diastolic blood pressure ≥80 mmHg, OR 2.58 vs. 1.43. However, formal interaction testing did not demonstrate statistically significant effect modification by CKD status. The sex-association model among patients with CKD demonstrated greater apparent discrimination than the corresponding non-CKD model (AUC, 0.785 vs. 0.630). Patients with AIS demonstrated distinct sex-associated clinical profiles according to CKD status. Although several associations were numerically stronger among patients with CKD, formal interaction testing did not establish statistically significant effect modification. These findings characterize clinical heterogeneity among men and women with established AIS and warrant further investigation to determine whether these profiles have implications for treatment or outcomes.

papers.title: Global trends and knowledge structure of cardiovascular magnetocardiography research: a bibliometric analysis.
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular diseases remain a leading global health threat. Recent advances in room-temperature sensing and artificial intelligence (AI) have renewed research interest in the clinical translation of magnetocardiography (MCG) for cardiovascular diagnosis, yet the global research evolution of MCG has yet to be quantitatively characterized. Literature from the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus (2000-2026) was analyzed using CiteSpace, VOSviewer, and R to evaluate publication trends, knowledge networks, and evolving frontiers. A total of 631 WoSCC and 755 Scopus articles were included. The publication trajectory exhibits a prolonged plateau followed by substantial recent growth. Germany, the United States, and China are the most prolific contributors. Keyword analysis revealed a diversification of technological and analytical themes. While early literature was strongly associated with superconducting quantum interference devices-based MCG, recent research has increasingly highlighted optically pumped magnetometers, magnetic-field control, sensor arrays, magnetic noise suppression, and AI-based signal analysis. The application landscape has broadened from physiological validation to coronary artery disease diagnosis, arrhythmia assessment, and fetal electrophysiology. Collectively, these findings suggest that the evolution of cardiovascular MCG reflects the parallel development and interaction of sensor technologies, AI-based analysis, and emerging clinical applications. Future research should prioritize standardized protocols, scalable and robust acquisition systems, and explainable AI models to accelerate clinical implementation.

papers.title: Effects of West Nile Virus on behavioral and cognitive performance, circadian body temperatures, cortical Aβ and p-tau pathology, and immune measures in human apoE and human amyloid precursor protein NL-G-F/human apoE mice.
papers.abstract: There are three human apolipoprotein E (E) isoforms: E2, E3, and E4. Compared with E3, E4 is an AD risk factor. West Nile Virus (WNV) can cause neurological disease, and it results in some neuropathology and neuroinflammation seen in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Previously, we reported on the effects of exposure to the Kunjin strain (KUNV) of WNV in middle-aged knock-in (KI) mice expressing human amyloid precursor protein (APP) containing the dominant NL-G-F mutations with human apoE targeted replacement (TR) mice on behavioral, immune, and pathological measures, and circadian body temperatures. NL-G-F/E4 mice were more susceptible to KUNV-induced cognitive injury and prolonged viral load in the cortex; viral load was detected in the cortex of more mice expressing amyloid precursor protein with the dominant NL-G-F AD mutations and expressing also E4 than those expressing also E3. As NL-G-F and NL-G-F/apoE mice show cognitive injury and neuropathology at 6 months of age and age is a risk factor to develop AD and modulates the immune response in AD, we assessed in this study whether genotype differences in response to KUNV exposure are seen in younger mice. To determine whether the presence of NL-G-F is required to detect genotype differences in response to KUNV and/or modulates the response to KUNV, E3 and E4 mice were included as well. As compared with E3, E2 reduces the risk to develop AD and the vast majority of AD would likely not occur in the absence of E3 and E4 NL-G-F/E2 mice were included in this study as well. We crossed knock-in (KI) mice expressing human amyloid precursor protein (APP) containing the dominant NL-G-F mutations with human apoE targeted replacement (TR) mice and used middle-aged NL-G-F/E3 and NL-G-F/E4 mice to assess the role of WNV (subtype Kunjin virus) (KUNV) exposure on behavioral alteration performance, circadian body temperatures, viral loads, neuropathology, and transcript levels of three immune measures in cortex important in the detrimental effects of KUNV on brain function. There were apoE isoform-dependent responses to KUNV exposure on various measures already seen at 6 months of age and are mostly more profound in the absence than in the presence of NL-G-F. One week following exposure, cortical insoluble p-tau levels were lower in KUNV- than PBS-treated apoE, but not NL-G-F/apoE mice. Soluble p-tau levels in cortex were higher in KUNV- than PBS-treated mice, and this effect was more pronounced in NL-G-F/apoE than apoE mice. The insoluble/soluble p-tau ratio was lower in KUNV- than PBS-treated mice, and this effect was more pronounced in apoE than NL-G-F/apoE. These results are consistent with results in cultured cells supporting that Aβ and p-tau might have antiviral properties.

papers.title: Selection on PER2 Phosphorylation Regulation Underlies Atypical Mammalian Circadian Rhythms.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms are fundamental biological processes that enhance survival and reproductive fitness by coordinating physiology and behavior with predictable environmental cycles. However, in some species, circadian rhythms are weakened, irregular, or even undetectable, likely reflecting evolutionary responses to extreme environments or specialized ecological niches. Nevertheless, the genetic basis of these atypical phenotypes remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the molecular evolution of 20 PER2-associated genes across 71 representative mammalian species. We identified four genes under positive selection in mammalian lineages exhibiting atypical circadian phenotypes, three of which (CDK5, CSNK1E, and GSK3B) are involved in the post-translational regulation of PER2 phosphorylation, suggesting that PER2 phosphorylation regulators may contribute to lineage-specific circadian variation. Notably, CSNK1E, a key kinase regulating PER2 phosphorylation, showed signatures of positive selection and accelerated evolution in cetaceans, which exhibit unihemispheric slow-wave sleep (USWS). In vitro assays showed that dolphin CSNK1E increased phosphorylation at the stabilizing FASP site S662 of PER2 and extended the half-life of the PER2 protein, a molecular feature closely linked to circadian oscillator amplitude and sleep regulation. Increased PER2 phosphorylation may contribute to altered sleep and locomotor activity associated with sustained wakefulness during USWS, as supported by our cellular and whole-animal assays. Consistently, zebrafish overexpressing dolphin CSNK1E exhibited elevated locomotor activity and reduced sleep duration. Overall, our findings provide evidence that evolutionary changes in PER2 phosphorylation regulation are associated with atypical circadian phenotypes and offer novel insights into the genetic mechanisms underlying circadian plasticity in mammals.

papers.title: Multiscale neural signatures of long-lag repetition learning: a simultaneous fNIRS-EEG study.
papers.abstract: Repetition-based learning supports word recognition and reading fluency, yet its neural mechanisms remain poorly understood, particularly where deficits in consolidating repeated linguistic input may underlie reading and language difficulties. Establishing reliable neural markers of repetition-based learning is a critical first step toward characterizing the phenotypes of these difficulties in children.
