papers.title: Molecular clockwork hypothesis for the KaiABC circadian oscillations.
papers.abstract: When three cyanobacterial proteins-KaiA, KaiB, and KaiC-are incubated with ATP in vitro, the phosphorylation level of KaiC exhibits stable circadian oscillations. Biochemical and structural analyses have shown that KaiC's ATPase activity is crucial for these oscillations, leading to the hypothesis that ATP-consuming dynamics function as a molecular clock, determining the oscillation period of individual molecules. Moreover, these molecular clocks synchronize collectively, resulting in oscillations at the ensemble level. In this study, we develop a theoretical model to test this molecular clockwork hypothesis. Our model clarifies the relationship between the oscillation period and ATPase activity, explaining the significant changes in the period induced by amino acid substitutions near the CI-CII domain boundary of the KaiC hexamer. Furthermore, the model addresses the physical basis for temperature compensation concerning both the oscillation period and ATPase activity. Thus, the molecular clockwork perspective provides a framework for understanding the atomic design behind collective oscillations.

papers.title: Frequency extraction from invariant flows.
papers.abstract: In nondegenerate integrable Hamiltonian systems, invariant tori can be parametrized by action variables or fundamental frequencies. We introduce an invariant-flow formulation, consistent with the Liouville-Arnold geometry, for extracting these frequencies. Treating invariants as generators of commuting Hamiltonian flows yields the frequencies from time-of-flight parameters, providing a direct alternative to action-angle constructions and long-time spectral analysis. The resulting numerical procedure extends naturally to multiple degrees of freedom and achieves high accuracy for the McMillan map. More broadly, the framework provides an invariant-centered view of near-integrable dynamics, recovering frequencies and other dynamical information from high-quality approximate invariants.

papers.title: Multivariate stochastic coupling in unknown complex systems: Informative randomness in deterministic brain-body communication.
papers.abstract: Physiological systems exhibit deterministic behavior influenced by dynamic stochasticity, where informative random components play a crucial role in complex system interactions. Fully characterizing multivariate random components is challenging when the underlying deterministic dynamics are unknown. We propose a framework for estimating stochastic coupling in unknown deterministic systems influenced by dynamic noise. Building on a multivariate extension of approximate entropy (MApEn), the proposed framework exploits the divergence of this metric in the presence of dynamical noise. After establishing the theoretical basis and validity of the method, which can accommodate arbitrary multivariate noise probability distributions, we show that, in the case of bivariate white Gaussian noise, the framework enables closed-form estimation of the noise covariance matrix without requiring prior knowledge of the underlying deterministic functions. To this end, we introduce an iterative algorithm to estimate the covariance matrix coefficients. The algorithm identifies the parameter values that rescale the differential behavior of multivariate MApEn along a target curve. We validate the framework using both synthetic datasets and real physiological recordings. The analysis reveals important insights into brain-heart interactions, particularly the modulation of stochastic coupling across sleep-stage transitions through low-frequency oscillatory activity. Our results indicate that conscious wakefulness is characterized by stronger stochastic coupling, which progressively decreases during the transition to sleep. This framework opens new avenues for investigating stochastic physiological dynamics and their associated networks, with potential applications across a wide range of scientific disciplines.

papers.title: GPU-accelerated sequential Monte Carlo for Bayesian spectral analysis.
papers.abstract: Bayesian spectral deconvolution provides a data-driven framework for mathematical model selection and parameter estimation from spectral data. Although highly versatile, its computational cost grows with the number of model parameters, data points, and candidate models, often rendering practical applications infeasible. We propose a GPU-accelerated approach in which a sequential Monte Carlo sampler (SMCS) is executed in parallel on a GPU to perform Bayesian model selection for the number of spectral peaks and Bayesian estimation of peak-function parameters. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the GPU-parallelized SMCS reaches the free-energy accuracy of an optimized CPU-parallelized replica exchange Monte Carlo (REMC) baseline up to approximately 37× faster-with smaller gains, down to near parity, in the least favorable settings-and is faster than GPU-parallelized REMC in many of the tested cases. The method is validated on artificial data designed to emulate x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and x-ray diffraction measurements, as well as on real experimental spectra. As measurement techniques such as microscopic spectroscopy and in situ methods continue to drive rapid growth in the volume of spectral data, the proposed approach offers a practical computational foundation for advanced analysis of each individual dataset.

papers.title: The characteristics of depression and sleep among Chinese high school students: A cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Mental health and sleep problems are among the most significant burdens of illnesses for adolescents in China. This study aimed to investigate the characteristics of depression and sleep quality among high school students and compare sleep quality across students with varying levels of depression. A cross-sectional study was performed to collect data on depression and sleep quality using a paper questionnaire including a self-rating depression scale (SDS) and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). Among all the 537 high school students, 57.0% (306 participants) experienced depression and 47.5% (255 participants) suffered from poor sleep quality. Males showed significantly greater SDS scores than females (55.2 ± 7.2 vs 53.8 ± 6.8, P = .027). Significantly greater PSQI score in high school students with moderate-to-severe depression than those with mild depression and nondepression (5.2 ± 2.7 vs 5.3 ± 2.4 vs 6.2 ± 2.3, F = 3.5, P = .032). In contrast, an adjusted logistic regression model indicated that depression severity was not an independent significant predictor of poor sleep quality after adjusting for age, sex, and BMI (all P > .05). Overall, high school students exhibited a high prevalence of depression and poor sleep quality, with those experiencing moderate-to-severe depression showing the poorest sleep quality in unadjusted comparisons. However, depression severity did not remain an independent significant predictor of poor sleep quality after adjustment. Depression and sleep problems among high school students should receive greater attention, particularly for high school students with moderate-to-severe depression.

papers.title: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation for the treatment of restless legs syndrome: A meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: The benefit of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) in patients with Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS) is uncertain. This study was performed to explore the therapeutic effect of rTMS in treating RLS. Databases including PubMed, EMbase, the Cochrane Library, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, and Wanfang database were searched from their inception to May 1, 2026. Eligible studies comparing rTMS with sham stimulation were included. Data were analyzed using Review Manager Version 5.3. Four studies were included in the meta-analysis. The overall pooled analysis confirmed that rTMS could effectively reduce International RLS-Rating Scale (IRLS-RS) scores (mean difference [MD] = 6.46, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 4.44 -8.48, P < .00001) and Pittsburgh sleep quality index (PSQI) scores (MD = 4.80, 95% CI: 3.51-6.08, P < .00001) at different follow-up periods. Meanwhile, the overall pooled analysis confirmed that rTMS could effectively reduce IRLS-RS scores (MD = 7.79, 95% CI: 3.90-11.68, P < .0001) and PSQI scores (MD = 5.58, 95% CI: 3.81-7.35, P < .00001) in the subgroup analysis by RLS subtype. However, rTMS showed no significant effect on PSQI scores in primary RLS (MD = 1.86, 95% CI: -2.65-6.37, P = .42). In addition, the overall pooled analysis confirmed that both low-frequency and high-frequency rTMS could effectively reduce IRLS-RS scores (MD = 7.79, 95% CI: 3.90-11.68, P < .0001) and PSQI scores (MD = 5.58, 95% CI: 3.81-7.35, P < .00001). Finally, the overall pooled analysis confirmed that rTMS could not significantly reduce Hamilton anxiety scale and Hamilton depression scale scores in subgroup analyses of follow-up period, RLS subtype, or rTMS frequency (P > .05). rTMS might alleviate core limb discomfort symptoms measured by IRLS-RS and improve sleep quality assessed by PSQI in patients with RLS. However, rTMS might not be effective in improving symptoms of anxiety and depression. To further confirm the conclusion, more large randomized controlled trials are necessary.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of the impact of neural stem cells on brain tumors.
papers.abstract: Malignant brain tumors, including glioblastoma and medulloblastoma, remain highly treatment-resistant. Neural stem cells (NSCs) are being investigated as tumor-tropic therapeutic vectors, but the temporal interaction between tumor and NSC populations requires quantitative characterization before model-based treatment hypotheses can be interpreted reliably. This study aimed to develop and numerically evaluate a reproducible 2-population model of tumor-NSC dynamics and to quantify the influence of NSC persistence and NSC-mediated tumor killing on simulated tumor burden. A normalized system of 2 coupled nonlinear ordinary differential equations was used: dT/dt = rT(1 - T) - βTN and dN/dt = αN(1 - N) - γTN. The baseline simulation used r = 0.20000 day-1, α = 0.05000 day-1, β = 0.35000 day-1, γ = 0.30000 day-1, T0 = 0.50000, and N0 = 0.40000. Explicit Euler integration was performed with Δt = 0.01 day over 20 days. A descriptive nonlinear regression fit, Fourier spectral analysis, 1-parameter sensitivity analyses, and joint α-β sensitivity analysis were applied to the simulated trajectory. In the baseline simulation, tumor density decreased from 0.5000 to a minimum of 0.4772 at day 2.59 (4.57% below the initial value) and subsequently increased to T20 = 0.8273, while NSC density declined from 0.4000 to N20 = 0.0247. The descriptive regression reproduced the simulated tumor trajectory with R2 = 0.9973 and root mean square error = 0.00590. Increasing α from 0.05 to 0.10 day-1 reduced T20 by 12.6% relative to baseline, and increasing β from 0.35 to 0.50 day-1 reduced T20 by 19.9%. Jointly setting α = 0.10 and β = 0.50 day-1 yielded T20 = 0.4427, 46.5% below the baseline terminal tumor density. The Fourier spectrum was dominated by the zero and low-frequency components, with no distinct oscillatory peak over the 20-day window. The model indicates that NSC persistence and NSC-mediated tumor killing materially influence terminal tumor burden, but the baseline parameterization produces only transient early suppression followed by tumor regrowth as the NSC population declines. The results are population-level, model-based estimates rather than tumor-type-specific clinical efficacy measures. Tumour-specific calibration, spatial migration, immune interactions, and experimental validation are required before translational conclusions can be drawn.

papers.title: Gut microbiota, sleep and coronary artery disease: A Mendelian randomization study.
papers.abstract: Inadequate and poor-quality sleep is increasingly recognized as a risk factor for coronary artery disease (CAD). Gut microbiota may play a role in sleep regulation. However, the associations between gut microbiota, sleep, and CAD risk, and the causal nature of these associations, remain unclear. We performed a 2-step Mendelian randomization analysis using summary-level data to assess the association between gut microbiota and CAD and the potential mediating roles of sleep-related traits (i.e., chronotype, insomnia, sleep duration, short sleep, and long sleep) herein. The inverse-variance weighted method served as the primary analysis, with several other complementary methods as sensitivity analyses. Our findings revealed that 2 gut microbial taxa were negatively associated with genetically predicted CAD risk, while 4 taxa, including species Veillonella unclassified (odds ratio: 1.054, 95% confidence interval: 1.010-1.101), showed positive associations. Regarding sleep-related traits, we found that insomnia (odds ratio: 1.553, 95% confidence interval: 1.081-2.230) and short sleep duration causally increased CAD risk, whereas longer sleep duration causally reduced CAD risk. The mediation Mendelian randomization analysis demonstrated that insomnia partially mediated the causal, predisposing effect of species Veillonella unclassified on increased CAD risk, with a proportion mediated of 5.7%. This study provides evidence for a causal relationship between specific gut microbial taxa and CAD risk, as well as the mediating role of insomnia in this relationship. These findings offer novel insights into potential strategies for CAD prevention through modulation of the gut microbiome and improvement of sleep quality.

papers.title: The effects of multiregional fascial mobilization on heart rate and physiological parameters in patients with obstructive sleep apnea: A randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is associated with increased sympathetic activity and an elevated cardiovascular risk. Noninvasive interventions targeting autonomic regulation may offer complementary therapeutic strategies. This randomized controlled trial aimed to investigate the acute effects of multiregional fascial mobilization on the physiological parameters of patients with OSA. Patients with polysomnography-confirmed moderate-to-severe OSA (apnea-hypopnea index ≥ 15 events/hour) were randomly assigned to an intervention group that received a standardized 16-minute multiregional fascial mobilization protocol or a control group that rested quietly in the supine position for the corresponding period without receiving manual or tactile intervention. The intervention targeted the cervical, thoracic, and abdominal regions, under controlled conditions. The primary outcomes included heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and peripheral oxygen saturation. Measurements were obtained at baseline, immediately post-intervention, and 5 and 15 minutes post-intervention. A total of 95 male patients (mean age: 48.12 ± 10.21 years) completed the study. Baseline characteristics were comparable between the groups, except for heart rate. After adjustment for baseline heart rate using mixed analysis of covariance, no significant group × time interaction was observed for heart rate (P = .476, partial ηp2 = .008). Similarly, no significant group × time interactions were observed for systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, or peripheral oxygen saturation (all P > .05). Although significant time effects were observed for some physiological parameters, the magnitude of these effects varied across outcomes, and none was accompanied by a significant group × time interaction. Therefore, these temporal changes were not interpreted as intervention-specific effects. No adverse events were reported. Heart rate changed significantly over time following the interventions; however, after adjustment for baseline heart rate, the pattern of change did not differ significantly between the fascial mobilization and control groups. Similarly, no significant between-group differences in changes over time were observed for blood pressure or oxygen saturation. These findings do not demonstrate a specific acute effect of multiregional fascial mobilization on the physiological parameters assessed. Further studies using advanced measures of autonomic function and longer follow-up periods are warranted.

papers.title: A cross-sectional study on the relationship between hepatitis C virus infection and the risk of sleep disorders among adults based on NHANES data from 2017 to 2020: A cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Patients with hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection often report sleep‑related complaints, but the relationship between HCV and clinically significant sleep disturbances remains poorly defined. This cross‑sectional study aimed to explore whether HCV infection is associated with an increased risk of sleep disorder among adults. Data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2017 to 2020 were analyzed. HCV infection status and sleep disorder were assessed using standardized questionnaires. Covariates including gender, age, race, marital status, alcohol use, body mass index, diabetes status, cancer history, and smoking status were adjusted in the analysis. A total of 7924 participants aged 20 to 80 years were enrolled, of whom 2310 had sleep disorder. The prevalence of HCV infection was significantly higher in participants with sleep disorder. After adjustment for potential confounders by multivariable logistic regression, HCV infection was independently associated with an increased risk of sleep disorder (odds ratio = 2.08; 95% confidence interval = 1.37-3.15; P < .05). HCV infection is significantly associated with an elevated risk of sleep disorder in adults. HCV screening among patients with sleep complaints may facilitate comprehensive clinical management.

papers.title: Individualized multimodal pain management for chronic perineal pain: A case report.
papers.abstract: Persistent perineal pain is a challenging clinical condition that may substantially impair sleep, urination, daily activities, and psychological well-being. Accurate assessment and individualized multimodal management are essential for improving symptom control and patient participation in care. A 68-year-old woman presented with chronic perineal pain and tenderness that had persisted for 3 years. The pain significantly interfered with her sleep, urination, and daily activities. Clinical assessment suggested chronic perineal pain with neuropathic involvement of the pudendal nerve and lumbosacral or sacral nerve roots. The diagnosis was established based on the patient's clinical manifestations, physical examination findings, and comprehensive evaluation. The patient received a multimodal pain management approach, including oral pregabalin, computed tomography-guided sacral canal catheterization with targeted nerve-root adhesiolysis and ozone injection, continuous pain assessment, psychological support, pelvic floor muscle training, and individualized rehabilitation guidance. At the two-week follow-up, the visual analog scale score decreased from 8/10 to 3/10, and the pain no longer interfered with sleep. Approximately 3 weeks after discharge, the pain temporarily increased to 5/10 and subsequently stabilized at 4/10 at the one-month follow-up while the patient continued oral pregabalin. Individualized multimodal pain management may effectively reduce pain intensity and improve sleep and daily functioning in patients with persistent perineal pain. Continuous assessment, patient participation, psychological support, and rehabilitation strategies are important components of comprehensive pain management.

papers.title: The bidirectional causal relationships of insomnia with eleven cancers: A Mendelian randomization study.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is closely associated with tumors and is recognized as a risk factor for cancer development. This two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) study investigated the potential causal link between genetically determined insomnia and various cancers, including brain, colorectal, esophageal, gastric, hepatic bile duct, liver, lung, malignant lymphoma, pancreatic, skin, and thyroid cancers. Summary statistics from genome-wide association studies for insomnia and eleven cancer types were examined. instrumental variables (IVs) were selected from single nucleotide polymorphisms that passed strict quality control for minimal linkage disequilibrium and genome-wide significance. All IVs demonstrated strong predictive power for insomnia, with F-statistics exceeding the conventional threshold of 10. The primary analysis was conducted using the inverse variance weighted method. Sensitivity analyses were performed using MR-Egger regression, weighted median, and weighted mode methods to test robustness, pleiotropy, and heterogeneity. MR analysis suggested potential causal associations between insomnia and increased risk of hepatic bile duct cancer (odds ratio [OR] = 4.458, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.074-18.493, P = .040), reduced risk of hepatic cancer (OR = 0.312, 95% CI: 0.100-0.973, P = .045), and reduced risk of skin cancers (OR = 0.599, 95% CI: 0.439-0.818, P = .001). However, after Bonferroni correction (adjusted threshold P < .0045), these associations did not retain statistical significance. No notable causal influence of these cancers on insomnia was observed. Sensitivity analyses showed no evidence of reverse causality or significant bias. These findings, though not retaining statistical significance after stringent multiple testing correction, provide suggestive evidence that genetically predicted insomnia may influence the risk of certain cancers, potentially through mechanisms involving genetic predisposition and biological pathways that modulate inflammation, immune function, and circadian rhythms. The study highlights the translational value of understanding insomnia's role in cancer risk, suggesting that clinicians should consider this association when managing patients with insomnia. Further research with larger sample sizes is warranted to validate these findings.

papers.title: Is cardiovascular autonomic control during the day-to-night transition dependent on dim light melatonin onset? An exploratory analysis in healthy adults.
papers.abstract: We tested whether dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO) is time-aligned with the transition between biological day into night in cardiovascular autonomic control (CV onset time). We studied 10 healthy adults (4 females, age 25 ± SD 2 years) under an ultra-short semi-constant routine protocol (<8lux). Participants remained seated for 7 h until 1 h after their habitual bedtime. We collected saliva samples every 30 min and recorded R-R intervals and beat-to-beat blood pressure every hour. DLMO was defined as the interpolated time for melatonin increase over 3 pg/mL. Phase angle was defined as the time difference between DLMO and the midpoint of self-reported sleep as a measure of the alignment between sleep-wake patterns and biological circadian rhythms. CV onset time was defined using a segmental (piecewise) analysis to identify the inflection point (X0 slope) throughout the study. CV autonomic modulation was assessed using indices of heart rate and blood pressure variability. CV onset times for all indices did not differ significantly from DLMO (p > 0.05). Mean differences between DLMO and CV onset time were significantly correlated with the phase angle of entrainment (all significant, r > +0.75). Our results suggest that CV autonomic transition into biological night was not associated with DLMO, which seems to depend on the phase angle of entrainment.

papers.title: Abdominal Tics in Children and Adolescents: A Phenomenology-First Diagnostic Framework and Differential Diagnosis.
papers.abstract: Abdominal tics are a less commonly described axial or tonic tic phenotype in children and adolescents with Tourette syndrome and chronic tic disorders. Their abdominal location and symptom language may create diagnostic uncertainty with gastrointestinal, epileptic, myoclonic, respiratory or functional presentations. This clinically focused narrative synthesis identified relevant literature through targeted searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Web of Science from database inception through March 2026, supplemented by a targeted PubMed/MEDLINE and citation-chasing update during revision through August 2026 focused on focal abdominal motor seizures, CASPR2-associated movement phenomena, peripheral nerve hyperexcitability and related mimics. Abdominal tics are supported by the same core tic features that apply across body regions: premonitory urge, partial suppressibility, stereotyped recurrence, waxing-and-waning course, sleep attenuation and prior or concurrent tics when present. Key neurological mimics include belly dancer's dyskinesia, propriospinal myoclonus, focal abdominal motor seizures, CASPR2-associated abdominal movement disorders and functional tic-like behaviours. Preserved awareness does not exclude a focal motor seizure. Gastrointestinal mimics include disorders of gut-brain interaction and inflammatory bowel disease. A pattern-directed clinical triage algorithm is proposed alongside management principles derived from established paediatric tic-disorder evidence, including behavioural intervention as first-line treatment and comorbidity-guided pharmacotherapy. A phenomenology-first, red-flag-guided approach can improve diagnostic clarity and help clinicians avoid both reflexive investigation and premature attribution of organic disease to tics. This review provides a practical clinical triage framework for determining when an abdominal movement behaves like a tic, when targeted neurological or gastrointestinal investigation is indicated and when management can follow established tic-disorder principles.

papers.title: Seizures Secondary to Aconitum Plant Poisoning: a case report.
papers.abstract: Aconitum plant poisoning typically manifests as isolated early cardiotoxicity or late neurotoxicity. However, the dynamic temporal evolution from arrhythmia-driven cardiogenic syncope to true epileptic seizures mediated by direct central nervous system injury remains rarely documented and poorly characterized. We report a 53-year-old Han Chinese male who presented with ventricular tachycardia rapidly degenerating into ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest following ingestion of homemade Aconitum kusnezoffii (caowu)-infused liquor. Initial convulsions were tightly coupled with malignant arrhythmias, consistent with cardiogenic syncope. After successful resuscitation, hemoperfusion, and restoration of stable sinus rhythm, the patient developed breakthrough generalized tonic-clonic seizures on hospital days 4-6. Electroencephalography performed during sedation withdrawal revealed bilateral occipital spike-and-slow and sharp-and-slow waves with focal epileptiform discharges, confirming direct central nervous system neurotoxicity rather than recurrent cardiac ischemia. A mechanism-based, staged treatment strategy was employed: early advanced cardiac life support and hemoperfusion targeted cardiotoxicity, while sodium valproate and acetylglutamine were administered for antiepileptic prophylaxis and neuroprotection. The patient was discharged on day 13; antiepileptic therapy was successfully tapered and discontinued at 3 months without seizure recurrence, with normalization of electroencephalography and electrocardiography. This case provides the first systematic documentation, validated by electroencephalography, of the transition from cardiogenic convulsions to true epileptic seizures in Aconitum alkaloid poisoning. The findings highlight the critical role of pharmacokinetic-driven central nervous system retention in delayed seizure onset and underscore the necessity of prolonged neurological monitoring, early electroencephalography evaluation for late-onset convulsions, and sustained antiepileptic prophylaxis to reduce mortality and long-term neurological sequelae. Aconitum plant poisoning may manifest as early cardiogenic syncope and convulsions secondary to malignant arrhythmias, progressing in the late stage to genuine seizures caused by central nervous system (CNS) injury. Effective management requires a staged treatment strategy targeting both cardiotoxicity and neurotoxicity, with a focus on stabilizing cardiac rhythm and providing neuroprotection as needed.

papers.title: Feasibility of unattended in-home polysomnography in trauma-exposed Veterans with chronic nightmares.
papers.abstract: This study examined the feasibility and acceptability of unattended home polysomnography (hPSG) in trauma-exposed U.S. Veterans with chronic nightmares (N = 47). Of the scheduled studies, 41 (87.2%) were completed. Twenty-four (58.5%) tests were successful based on all pre-specified criteria. Twenty-nine (71%) had ≥4 hours of interpretable EEG. No baseline differences were found between Veterans with and without successful hPSGs. Regarding acceptability, sleep quality was rated significantly worse on the night with hPSG compared to a night without. This study observed that unattended hPSG is partially feasible and acceptable in a group of trauma-exposed Veterans; however, failure was common. Characteristics of trauma-exposed samples, such as increased sweating and sleep movements, may have contributed to these results. Tools designed to be applied independently and to endure these factors should be considered.
